title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry

paper.title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry
paper.abstract: Abstract In 3D computer vision, geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and subsequently align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from previous frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when subsequent observations reveal errors. To address these limitations, we introduce S caffold M em O ry for Re vision ( SMoRe ), a framework that equips existing geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMoRe associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. Crucially, SMoRe integrates with existing geometry foundation models while keeping them frozen, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. We evaluate SMoRe with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all the evaluated geometry models, SMoRe consistently improves long-sequence camera pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected camera poses and observations, SMoRe further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences. Code, data, and models will be publicly available upon publication.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction and Related Work
sections.text: Recovering camera motion and 3D scene structure from visual observations is fundamental to 3D computer vision, underpinning robotic navigation, autonomous systems, augmented reality, and embodied AI Shen et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026c) ; Piriyajitakonkij et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2018b) ; Zhang et al. (2018a) ; Khandelwal et al. (2023) . Recent geometry foundation models have made substantial progress toward this goal. DUSt3R ( Wang et al., 2024b ) introduced point-map regression for unified geometric inference without known camera calibration or poses, followed by MASt3R ( Leroy et al., 2024 ) , Fast3R ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , VGGT ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , VGGT- Ω \Omega ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , and π 3 \pi^{3} ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . These models estimate camera poses, depth, correspondences, and 3D scene structure directly from images. Yet, a fundamental challenge remains: how can they maintain accurate, spatially consistent reconstructions over long horizons? Existing geometry models largely approach long sequences in two ways, both with important limitations (Fig. 1 ). First, feed-forward models such as VGGT, VGGT- Ω \Omega , and π 3 \pi^{3} ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026b ) jointly infer geometry from groups of images. Long sequences are divided into fixed-length windows, reconstructed separately, and subsequently aligned into a common coordinate system. Small reconstruction or alignment errors can accumulate across windows, degrading camera poses and 3D geometry over long trajectories. TALO ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) and AMB3R ( Wang and Agapito, 2026 ) address this through submap alignment and compact volumetric representations, respectively, while VGGSfM ( Wang et al., 2024a ) and GlueMap ( Pan et al., 2026 ) combine learned geometry with structure-from-motion. Nevertheless, long-horizon reconstruction still requires maintaining geometric consistency across observations or submaps. Second, streaming geometry models such as CUT3R ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , StreamVGGT ( Zhuo et al., 2026 ) , and STream3R ( Lan et al., 2026 ) maintain information across successive observations through persistent states or causal caches. Such memory allows previous observations to inform future predictions, but retaining past context and explicitly revising previously estimated camera poses and scene geometry are different capabilities. Relatedly, EAGLE ( Cao et al., 2026 ) combines visual and geometric memory for visual-query localization in egocentric video, but does not target retrospective correction of long-horizon 3D reconstruction. Later observations may reveal that an earlier estimate was incorrect, yet existing streaming memory does not explicitly retrieve, verify, and revise that estimate. Thus, remembering the past is not equivalent to revising it. The need for retrospective correction is well established in simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), where errors are corrected through loop closure and global optimization, as in graph-based SLAM ( Grisetti et al., 2010 ; Strasdat et al., 2010 ) , ElasticFusion ( Whelan et al., 2015 ) , and ORB-SLAM3 ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Learned systems such as DROID-SLAM ( Teed and Deng, 2021 ) , NICER-SLAM ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) , and SLAMFormer ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) exploit geometric constraints across observations to correct accumulated errors. More recent works, including MASt3R-SLAM ( Murai et al., 2025 ) , VGGT-SLAM ( Maggio et al., 2025 ) , VGGT-SLAM++ ( Mandal et al., 2026 ) , and ViSTA-SLAM ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , combine learned geometry with loop closure, while VGGT-SLAM 2.0 ( Maggio and Carlone, 2026 ) uses model attention to verify retrieved images. However, these are dedicated SLAM systems built around specific representations and optimization pipelines. This motivates a general question: can existing geometry foundation models be equipped with a shared external memory to recall, verify, and revise past predictions while remaining frozen? Beyond computer vision, recurrent neural fields and continuous attractor networks (CANs) in neuroscience provide biologically inspired mechanisms for maintaining and representing continuous variables through persistent neural activity ( Amari, 1977 ; Burak and Fiete, 2009 ) . Vector-HaSH ( Chandra et al., 2025 ) further combines structured spatial representations with associative memory, linking spatial states with sensory observations. This principle suggests a natural way to organize long-horizon visual memory: associate where an observer is with what it observes, so that past observations can be retrieved when related spatial states are revisited. Building on this principle, we introduce S caffold M em O ry for Re vision ( SMoRe ), a revisable external memory for extending existing geometry foundation models to long-horizon inference. SMoRe goes beyond associative retrieval by supporting an explicit cycle of storage, retrieval, verification, and revision . As new observations arrive, SMoRe retrieves relevant past observations, compares them with current geometric evidence, verifies their consistency, and revises previously estimated poses and geometry when inconsistencies are detected. Corrected observations are retained in memory and can subsequently provide improved geometric context for later inference. Importantly, SMoRe is external to the geometry backbone. It therefore does not require a new geometry model to be trained for long-horizon processing. Instead, existing geometry foundation models can be integrated with SMoRe while their model weights remain frozen, requiring neither additional training nor fine-tuning. This design separates the problem of learning strong geometric priors from the problem of maintaining and correcting information over time: the foundation model provides geometric inference, while SMoRe provides persistent and revisable memory. Consequently, the same memory framework can be applied across different geometry backbones and tasks. We evaluate SMoRe with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across the evaluated geometry models, incorporating SMoRe consistently improves long-sequence camera pose estimation. It reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. The corrected poses and observations retained by SMoRe further improve the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. Our contributions are threefold: 1. Revisable external memory for long-horizon 3D geometry. We introduce SMoRe , an external memory that associates spatial context with visual observations and supports explicit storage, retrieval, geometric verification, and revision of previously estimated poses and scene structure. 2. Training-free integration with frozen geometry foundation models. SMoRe provides a model-agnostic interface for augmenting existing geometry foundation models while keeping their weights frozen, enabling long-horizon error correction without additional training or fine-tuning. 3. Comprehensive evaluation across models and 3D tasks. We evaluate SMoRe with eight geometry models on five datasets across camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, SLAM, and novel view synthesis, demonstrating consistent improvements in long-horizon geometric accuracy and spatial consistency.

sections.heading:
2 Our Proposed S caffold M em O ry
for Re vision ( SMoRe )
sections.text: We introduce SMoRe , a revisable external memory for extending pretrained geometry foundation models to long-horizon inference (Fig. 1 ). SMoRe consists of a spatial scaffold and a content bank . The content bank stores past observations and their geometric predictions, while the scaffold associates where an observation was captured with what was observed through a shared memory representation. As new observations arrive, SMoRe stores their spatial and visual representations and uses visual content to retrieve candidate revisits. Because associative retrieval alone cannot determine whether a candidate is a genuine revisit, retrieved observations are verified against their historical poses before being used for correction. A verified revisit provides a global spatial anchor for revising accumulated placement errors. The geometry foundation model remains frozen throughout; only the external memory is updated online. Before describing these memory operations, we first define the overlapping frame windows used for local reconstruction and the local and global coordinate systems used to place and revise these reconstructions. Given RGB frames I 1 , … , I N I_{1},\ldots,I_{N} , we process them in overlapping windows 𝒲 k \mathcal{W}_{k} . By default, each window contains 32 frames, with 16 shared between consecutive windows. See Table S4 (Group G) for the effect of window size and overlap. Because a frame can appear in two overlapping windows, it is stored only once, using the first window in which it appears. We call this its source window , denoted src ⁡ ( i ) \operatorname{src}(i) for frame I i I_{i} . For each window, the geometry foundation model predicts camera poses and 3D point maps in a local coordinate system defined by the camera pose of the first frame in that window. We define the global coordinate system as that of the first window and let T k ∈ Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) T_{k}\in\mathrm{Sim}(3) denote the transformation that places 𝒲 k \mathcal{W}_{k} in this global coordinate system. Consecutive windows are initially placed by aligning the predicted camera poses of their overlapping frames. Camera poses and point maps remain stored in their source window’s local coordinate system, while T k T_{k} determines their global placement. The robust similarity alignment and the effect of changing T k T_{k} on stored geometry are detailed in Appendices B and C .

sections.heading: 2.1 Associating Spatial and Visual Memory
sections.text: After processing each window, SMoRe stores its new frames in the content bank together with their predicted camera poses and point maps. Rather than storing global poses in a lookup table indexed by frame identity, SMoRe builds an associative memory : spatial states and visual observations are linked through a shared memory representation. This is important because, at retrieval time, the identity and location of a revisited frame are unknown. A new visual observation must therefore serve as a partial cue for recalling previously associated spatial information.

sections.heading: Spatial scaffold.
sections.text: Following Vector-HaSH ( Chandra et al., 2025 ) , we represent each frame’s global camera pose using a structured spatial scaffold. Camera position is encoded by three periodic spatial modules operating at different spatial scales, while yaw, pitch, and roll are represented by three continuous attractor rings. The periodic representation preserves the continuous structure of position and orientation, while combining multiple spatial scales reduces the ambiguity introduced by any single periodic representation. Their concatenation forms the scaffold state 𝐠 i \mathbf{g}_{i} . We map 𝐠 i \mathbf{g}_{i} through a fixed random linear projection to a 1024-dimensional memory representation 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} , retaining only the 64 largest activations followed by normalization. This sparse intermediate representation is a deliberate design choice: activating only a small subset of memory units reduces interference among stored associations, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and making recall more robust to partial or noisy cues. We systematically vary the sparsity level and scaffold dimension and study their effects in Table S4 (Groups B and D). A reverse mapping, learned using ridge regression, reconstructs the spatial scaffold state from 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} . Thus, unlike a lookup table that can only return an entry given its explicit index, the scaffold supports associative reconstruction of spatial information from a shared memory state (see more analysis in Appendix J.1 and Table S4 (Group A)). See Appendix D for details of scaffold encoding and projection.

sections.heading: Associating visual observations with the scaffold.
sections.text: To connect what is observed with where it was observed, we encode each frame I i I_{i} using a frozen DINOv2 ViT-S/14 encoder ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , yielding a normalized 384-dimensional visual descriptor 𝐬 i \mathbf{s}_{i} . We learn bidirectional associations between 𝐬 i \mathbf{s}_{i} and the shared memory representation 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} : visual content can cue its associated memory state, while the memory state can reconstruct its associated visual representation. Both mappings are updated incrementally using recursive least squares (RLS) whenever a new frame is stored. Together, these associations connect the spatial scaffold state 𝐠 i \mathbf{g}_{i} , shared memory representation 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} , and visual descriptor 𝐬 i \mathbf{s}_{i} . Consequently, a new visual observation can provide a partial cue for recalling memories associated with similar past observations, rather than requiring the identity or location of the corresponding frame to be known in advance. This associative recall is central to SMoRe : it enables what is currently observed to cue where related observations were previously encountered. Because such recall alone cannot establish that two observations correspond to the same physical location, we use it only to propose candidate revisits, which are subsequently verified geometrically (Sec. 2.2 ). All memory updates are external to the pretrained models; the geometry foundation model and DINOv2 encoder remain frozen. Instead of DINOv2, we evaluate alternative visual features in Appendix J.2 and Table S4 (Group C).

sections.heading: 2.2 Retrieving and Verifying Revisits for Window Revision
sections.text: Retrieving candidate revisits based on visual feature similarity. Given a current frame I q I_{q} , we compute its visual descriptor 𝐬 q \mathbf{s}_{q} and use the learned visual association to obtain a query memory representation 𝐡 ~ q \widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{q} . Retrieval uses only visual information; the current camera pose and 3D geometry are not used. We do not directly trust the spatial state recalled from 𝐡 ~ q \widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{q} , because a novel observation may still activate an existing memory. Instead, we compare 𝐡 ~ q \widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{q} with all stored memory representations and select the five most similar frames. We then remove candidates that are within 64 frames of the current observation, originate from the immediately preceding window, or have DINOv2 cosine similarity below 0.5 0.5 . The remaining frames are treated as candidate revisits and are geometrically verified next. Full retrieval details are provided in Appendix D . Verifying revisits by historical pose consistency. For each retrieved candidate, we select a second nearby frame ( ± 3 \pm 3 frames) from the same source window to form a retrieved pair . We retain two pairs from different source windows, providing two independent historical references. If fewer than two valid pairs are available, no retrieval-based correction is applied. We use two pairs by default and study this choice in Table S4 (Group E). When two pairs are available, the geometry foundation model jointly processes the 32 current-window frames and four retrieved frames, placing all 36 frames in a common local coordinate system. The current window retains this joint prediction unless it rotates the current frames by more than 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} relative to the prediction from the current window alone, in which case the current-window prediction is kept and the joint pass serves only to measure the revisit (Appendix M ). Each retrieved pair connects this joint prediction to its previously placed source window and independently proposes a global placement for the current window, denoted T k ( a ) T_{k}^{(a)} and T k ( b ) T_{k}^{(b)} . We accept the revisit only if the two proposals are consistent in both rotation and translation: their rotational difference must be at most 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} , and their positional difference must be at most the spatial extent E k E_{k} of the current reconstruction (the median distance of its cameras from their centroid). Otherwise, the retrieval is rejected. Once verified, all four retrieved frames are jointly used to robustly estimate a single corrected global placement T k corr T_{k}^{\mathrm{corr}} . Importantly, T k corr T_{k}^{\mathrm{corr}} is fitted jointly from both historical references rather than obtained by averaging T k ( a ) T_{k}^{(a)} and T k ( b ) T_{k}^{(b)} . The alignment, verification, and corrected-placement formulations are provided in Appendix F . Progressive placement revision along the trajectory. The difference between the original placement T k T_{k} and corrected placement T k corr T_{k}^{\mathrm{corr}} represents the accumulated placement error revealed by the revisit. Rather than applying the correction abruptly to the current window, we progressively distribute it across the windows between the earlier historical reference and the current window. The historical reference remains fixed, intermediate windows receive increasingly larger corrections, and the current window receives the full correction. We interpolate these corrections in Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) ; the full formulation is provided in Appendix G . See Appendix J.3 and Table S4 (Group F) for an analysis of alternative placement revision strategies. Only the global placement of each affected window is revised. Its stored camera poses and point maps remain expressed in the local coordinate system of its source window and therefore move together under the updated global placement.

sections.heading: 3 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate all competitive baselines with and without SMoRe across five downstream tasks: camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. We perform three runs per experiment and aggregate results across runs. For each task, we describe the problem setting and datasets, followed by the compared methods, metrics, and results. Unless otherwise stated, all main-paper SMoRe results use only online retrieval, verification, and revision, without offline global optimization. We focus on this more challenging and practical setting, where corrections are made as observations arrive without access to the complete sequence. Results with offline pose-graph optimization are provided in Appendix J .

sections.heading: Problem setting and datasets.
sections.text: We evaluate long-horizon camera pose estimation on CO3Dv2 ( Reizenstein et al., 2021 ) and RealEstate10K (RE10K) ( Zhou et al., 2018 ) . CO3Dv2 contains object-centric videos spanning 8–68 s, with 200 annotated frames per sequence. RE10K contains predominantly forward-moving real-estate videos; we use 100 clips spanning 6.7–9.3 s. For both datasets, we uniformly sample N ∈ { 10 , 50 , 100 , 200 } N\in\{10,50,100,200\} frames from each trajectory. Baselines. We evaluate six feed-forward geometry foundation models: DUSt3R ( Wang et al., 2024b ) , Fast3R ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , MASt3R ( Leroy et al., 2024 ) , VGGT ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , VGGT- Ω \Omega ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , and π 3 \pi^{3} ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , together with two streaming models: StreamVGGT ( Zhuo et al., 2026 ) and STream3R ( Lan et al., 2026 ) . For each model, we compare its original camera predictions with those obtained using SMoRe on identical sampled frames. Feed-forward models use 32-frame windows with and without SMoRe . Streaming baselines use their native causal inference, while their SMoRe variants use the same 32-frame windowing policy. Metrics. We evaluate all pairs of sampled frames. For each pair, pose error is the larger of the rotation and translation-direction errors, so lower is better. AUC@30 instead measures the normalized area under the cumulative fraction of frame pairs whose pose error falls below thresholds up to 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} ; therefore, higher AUC@30 is better. Results. As shown in the right panel of Fig. 2 A, SMoRe consistently improves camera pose estimation on CO3Dv2, with nearly all points lying above the diagonal. The gains become more pronounced for longer sequences, with larger markers generally farther above the diagonal. At N = 200 N=200 , for example, VGGT improves from 90.0 to 93.9 AUC, VGGT- Ω \Omega from 91.6 to 94.7, and π 3 \pi^{3} from 89.9 to 93.3. On RE10K (left), the gains are smaller but remain evident across sequence lengths, including shorter trajectories. This is consistent with its predominantly forward camera motion providing fewer opportunities to revisit previously observed regions. Notably, some streaming baselines run out of memory (OOM) on longer sequences in both datasets, whereas the same models equipped with SMoRe successfully perform camera pose estimation through memory-efficient windowed processing (crosses in Fig. 2 A). sections.heading: 3.2 Multi-view Depth Estimation and 3D Point-Cloud Reconstruction
sections.text: Problem setting and datasets. We evaluate multi-view depth estimation on Replica ( Straub et al., 2019 ) and 3D point-cloud reconstruction on ScanNet++ ( Yeshwanth et al., 2023 ) . Replica contains 18 photorealistic synthetic indoor environments with approximately 2,000 frames per scene, providing long camera trajectories and dense reference geometry for multi-view depth evaluation. ScanNet++ contains 1,006 high-fidelity real-world indoor scenes with high-resolution RGB observations and laser-scanned reference geometry, with long sequences spanning each indoor environment. For both datasets, we process the sequences using the 32-frame windowing strategy in Sec. 2 . These long sequences require reconstruction across many successive windows, providing a challenging setting for evaluating whether SMoRe can reduce accumulated geometric inconsistencies through revisited observations. Baselines. We use the same eight geometry models (Sec. 3.1 ), comparing each baseline with its SMoRe counterpart. Metrics. We report reconstruction accuracy, completeness, and overall error in centimetres. Accuracy measures the distance from reconstructed to reference geometry, while completeness measures the reverse direction. Overall error is their mean; lower is better.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Table 1 shows consistent improvements with SMoRe across all eight geometry models on both datasets when evaluated over full trajectories. On Replica, SMoRe reduces overall Chamfer error by approximately 58% across the evaluated models. For example, VGGT improves from 9.15 to 2.49 cm and VGGT- Ω \Omega from 7.50 to 2.00 cm. On ScanNet++, SMoRe cuts baseline trajectory drift substantially: VGGT improves from 24.95 to 6.05 cm and VGGT- Ω \Omega from 20.80 to 4.95 cm. Streaming models also exhibit marked gains (e.g., StreamVGGT overall error drops from 6.65 to 1.84 cm on Replica and from 17.80 to 4.50 cm on ScanNet++). These results confirm that revising previously placed window reconstructions with SMoRe successfully resolves accumulated drift over long sequences. sections.heading: Problem setting and dataset.
sections.text: We evaluate SLAM on all seven indoor scenes of 7-Scenes ( Shotton et al., 2013 ) , where the objective is to estimate the camera trajectory while reconstructing the environment from an incoming video stream. Each sequence contains 17–33 s of continuous video, providing long trajectories for evaluating accumulated drift and revisit-driven correction. Baselines. We compare against published calibrated and uncalibrated SLAM methods: NICER-SLAM ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) , DROID-SLAM ( Teed and Deng, 2021 ) , MASt3R-SLAM ( Murai et al., 2025 ) , GLUEMAP ( Pan et al., 2026 ) , TALO ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , VGGT-SLAM++ ( Mandal et al., 2026 ) , ViSTA-SLAM ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , SLAM-Former ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , CUT3R ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , VGGT-SLAM ( Maggio et al., 2025 ) with Sim(3) and L(4), VGGSfM ( Wang et al., 2024a ) , and VGGT- Ω \Omega ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . Published baselines retain their reported protocols. Calibrated methods receive ground-truth camera intrinsics, whereas uncalibrated methods estimate them from the input frames. We compare the uncalibrated VGGT- Ω \Omega baseline with uncalibrated VGGT- Ω \Omega + SMoRe . Metrics. We report absolute trajectory error (ATE) RMSE in metres after similarity alignment between the estimated and ground-truth camera trajectories. This alignment removes global scale differences, enabling fair comparison across methods; lower is better.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: As shown in Fig. 3 A, SMoRe reduces the average ATE RMSE of VGGT- Ω \Omega from 4.5 to 2.9 cm. Notably, this is lower than the best reported calibrated baseline using ground-truth camera intrinsics (3.1 cm) and the best reported uncalibrated baseline (3.8 cm). These results show that revisit-driven revision with SMoRe improves long-horizon trajectory consistency without fine-tuning the geometry foundation model. Fig. 3 B visualizes the resulting 3D reconstruction for an example 7-Scenes sequence. We transform the predicted local point maps into the global coordinate system using the estimated camera poses and stitch them into a single reconstruction. Chaining VGGT- Ω \Omega predictions accumulates placement errors, resulting in visible misalignment around the cabinet and countertop. In contrast, SMoRe uses revisited observations to correct their global placement, producing a more spatially consistent reconstruction with finer geometric details. Fig. 3 C shows the pairwise positional error between frames. SMoRe reduces the average pairwise error from 8.1 to 6.5 cm. The improvement is particularly evident for temporally distant frame pairs (red boxes), where chained VGGT- Ω \Omega exhibits larger errors than its SMoRe counterpart. This demonstrates that SMoRe better preserves geometric consistency between observations separated by long temporal intervals. Finally, Fig. 3 D shows the positional error over time. VGGT- Ω + \Omega+ SMoRe generally maintains lower error than VGGT- Ω \Omega throughout the sequence, with particularly pronounced reductions following verified revisits (green lines). sections.heading: Problem setting and datasets.
sections.text: We evaluate novel view synthesis on 7-Scenes ( Shotton et al., 2013 ) and CO3Dv2 ( Reizenstein et al., 2021 ) , where input views from long sequences are used to render scenes from unseen viewpoints. Every eighth keyframe is held out for evaluation and excluded from geometry prediction. We evaluate 156 held-out views on 7-Scenes and 888 on CO3Dv2 (Appendix H.5 ). Baselines. We compare VGGT- Ω \Omega , VGGT, π 3 \pi^{3} , STream3R, Fast3R, and StreamVGGT ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Lan et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Zhuo et al., 2026 ) . For each geometry model, we train separate 3D Gaussian decoders using geometry from chained consecutive windows (Baseline) and SMoRe , respectively. For fair comparison, both decoders share the same architecture, training data, schedule, and random seed. Each decoder renders target views from eight nearby input keyframes, while the geometry models remain frozen. Decoders are trained on 7-Scenes sequences disjoint from test trajectories and transferred to CO3Dv2 without further fine-tuning (Appendix I ). Metrics. We report PSNR ( ↑ \uparrow ), SSIM ( ↑ \uparrow ), and LPIPS ( ↓ \downarrow ). To assess long-horizon consistency, we additionally analyze target views whose source keyframes span multiple visits to the same region (Appendix H.5 ).

sections.text: As shown in Table 2 , SMoRe improves all three metrics across all six geometry models on 7-Scenes, with larger gains for revisited targets (Appendix I ). On CO3Dv2, VGGT- Ω \Omega , VGGT, π 3 \pi^{3} , and StreamVGGT achieve PSNR gains of 0.34–0.64 dB with SMoRe , alongside improvements in SSIM and LPIPS. STream3R and Fast3R achieve comparable PSNR with and without SMoRe , while improving SSIM and LPIPS with SMoRe . These smaller gains may reflect residual errors in local geometric predictions that cannot be corrected through window placement revision alone. Qualitative examples are shown in Fig. 2 B and Fig. S2 . In Fig. 2 B, for example, VGGT- Ω \Omega + SMoRe better preserves the geometry and appearance of the headphone than VGGT- Ω \Omega alone. More generally, the improved geometry yields sharper object boundaries and better-preserved object structure in the synthesized views. sections.heading: 3.5 Design Choices and Computational Requirements
sections.text: We analyze key design choices of SMoRe on 7-Scenes SLAM (ATE RMSE, ↓ \downarrow ) and CO3Dv2 camera pose estimation (AUC@30, ↑ \uparrow ). We group the results by design factor in Table S4 , with full results provided in Appendix J . From Table S4 , we observe: Memory scaffold (Group A). Replacing our associative scaffold with a lookup table degrades performance, supporting associative memory as a more effective structure for memory storage, retrieval, and revision. Memory sparsity (Group B). Varying the sparsity of 𝐡 \mathbf{h} reveals a trade-off between sparse coding and information preservation, with our default providing a good balance. Visual descriptors (Group C). We compare DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) with alternative visual descriptors (Appendix J.2 ). DINOv2 performs best, highlighting the importance of strong visual representations for reliable candidate retrieval. Scaffold dimension (Group D). Performance is stable across the tested dimensions, with smaller dimensions slightly degrading performance and larger ones providing limited additional gains. Retrieval evidence (Group E). Too little retrieval evidence degrades performance, while additional pairs provide diminishing gains, motivating our default setting. Progressive placement revision (Group F). Progressive correction in SMoRe outperforms uniformly distributing the correction along the trajectory, suggesting that larger corrections should be applied to more recent frames. Window size and overlap (Group G). Larger windows and greater overlap generally improve performance but increase computational and memory costs, motivating our default choice of 32-frame windows with 16 overlapping frames (50% overlap). Computational requirements. We evaluate the GPU memory, CPU memory, RAM size, PFLOPs, and runtime of geometry foundation models with and without SMoRe (Appendix K.1 ). In Table S5 , as sequence length N N increases, SMoRe keeps the geometry model’s active GPU working set largely bounded because inference operates on fixed-size windows and retrieves only a small number of historical frames when needed. In contrast, feed-forward baselines must maintain intermediate predictions to chain consecutive windows, while streaming models retain growing causal states or caches and can eventually exceed GPU memory limits. Although the external memory of SMoRe grows with the stored visual history, this growth occurs primarily outside the geometry model’s active GPU context, allowing long sequences to be processed with substantially better memory scalability. Reducing peak GPU memory does not make SMoRe computationally free; instead, it trades a bounded GPU working set for additional memory management. Table S6 shows that computation in GPU remain dominated by the underlying geometry foundation model, while SMoRe adds modest CPU, PFLOP, and runtime overhead. In return, SMoRe enables substantially better memory scaling; for example, STream3R runs out of GPU memory at N = 100 N=100 , whereas STream3R+ SMoRe can still process the full sequence using bounded-window inference.

sections.heading: 4 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: We introduced SMoRe , a revisable external memory that extends frozen geometry foundation models beyond fixed-context prediction through storage, retrieval, geometric verification, and revision. Across eight geometry models, five datasets, and five downstream tasks, our results show that SMoRe complements both feed-forward and streaming models, using verified revisits to correct accumulated errors over long visual sequences without fine-tuning the underlying geometry models. Several directions remain for future work. Retrieval verification introduces additional computation, motivating more efficient mechanisms for recalling reliable spatial information from the memory scaffold. Moreover, SMoRe currently focuses on revising global window placement; future work could extend revision to local geometric predictions when later observations provide stronger evidence.

sections.text: The shared-frame alignment between consecutive windows normally has multiple camera correspondences. A retrieved pair in Sec. 2.2 , however, contains only two cameras. Two camera centres determine a baseline but do not by themselves uniquely constrain rotation about that baseline. The camera-orientation check provides additional consistency information, and SMoRe further requires two retrieved pairs from different source windows to produce consistent global-placement proposals before accepting a revisit.

sections.heading: Appendix C Window Ownership and Geometric Invariance
sections.text: In Sec. 2.1 , each frame is stored once using its source window, and its camera pose and point map remain in that window’s local coordinate system. Later, Sec. 2.2 changes only the global placement T k T_{k} of a window. Here we make explicit what this means for the stored geometry and for relative camera poses.

sections.heading: Source-window storage.
sections.text: Because consecutive windows overlap, the same frame may be predicted in more than one window. We store it only once, using the first window in which it appears. For frame I i I_{i} , this window is 𝒲 src ⁡ ( i ) \mathcal{W}_{\operatorname{src}(i)} . Suppose I i I_{i} is stored in source window 𝒲 k \mathcal{W}_{k} , with local camera pose ( R i , c i ) (R_{i},c_{i}) and local 3D points x i x_{i} . These quantities remain fixed in the coordinate system of 𝒲 k \mathcal{W}_{k} . Their global values are obtained only when the window placement T k = ( a k , Q k , 𝐛 k ) T_{k}=(a_{k},Q_{k},\mathbf{b}_{k}) is applied: R i global = Q k ​ R i , c i global = a k ​ Q k ​ c i + 𝐛 k , R_{i}^{\mathrm{global}}=Q_{k}R_{i},\qquad c_{i}^{\mathrm{global}}=a_{k}Q_{k}c_{i}+\mathbf{b}_{k}, and x i global = a k ​ Q k ​ x i + 𝐛 k . x_{i}^{\mathrm{global}}=a_{k}Q_{k}x_{i}+\mathbf{b}_{k}. Thus, the content bank stores local geometry, while T k T_{k} determines where that geometry currently lies in the global reconstruction.

sections.heading: What changes after a placement correction?
sections.text: When Sec. 2.2 replaces T k T_{k} by an updated global placement, the stored local camera poses and point maps are not recomputed. Instead, the new transformation is applied to the same local quantities. Consequently, all cameras and 3D points belonging to 𝒲 k \mathcal{W}_{k} move together. This separation is useful because a revisit can correct where a window is placed without modifying the geometric relationships already predicted inside that window.

sections.heading: Relative poses within one source window.
sections.text: Consider two frames I i I_{i} and I j I_{j} stored in the same source window 𝒲 k \mathcal{W}_{k} . After applying T k T_{k} , their global rotations satisfy ( R j global ) ⊤ ​ R i global = R j ⊤ ​ R i . \left(R_{j}^{\mathrm{global}}\right)^{\top}R_{i}^{\mathrm{global}}=R_{j}^{\top}R_{i}. Their relative translation, expressed in frame I j I_{j} , becomes ( R j global ) ⊤ ​ ( c i global − c j global ) = a k ​ R j ⊤ ​ ( c i − c j ) . \left(R_{j}^{\mathrm{global}}\right)^{\top}\left(c_{i}^{\mathrm{global}}-c_{j}^{\mathrm{global}}\right)=a_{k}R_{j}^{\top}(c_{i}-c_{j}). Therefore, changing T k T_{k} leaves their relative rotation and translation direction unchanged. Only the translation magnitude can change through the window scale a k a_{k} . This is why a placement correction primarily changes relationships between windows rather than the relative camera geometry already stored within one source window. It also explains why the pairwise-pose metric, which uses rotation and translation-direction errors, is unchanged for two frames whose local predictions remain fixed in the same source window.

sections.heading: When this property does not apply.
sections.text: The argument above assumes that the stored local predictions ( R i , c i ) (R_{i},c_{i}) themselves are unchanged. In Sec. 2.2 , however, processing retrieved frames jointly with the current window can also produce new local camera poses and point maps. That is a separate effect from changing T k T_{k} . Appendix M isolates these two sources of change experimentally.

sections.heading: Appendix D Scaffold Construction, Storage, and Retrieval
sections.text: Sections 2.1 and 2.2 introduce the two memory operations used by SMoRe . When a frame is stored, its estimated global camera pose is converted into a compact memory address. Later, the visual content of a current frame is used to predict an address and retrieve previously stored frames. Here we explain how the pose representation, memory address, and visual descriptor are connected, why the scaffold uses multiple spatial scales and a sparse address, and which parts of this associative pathway are actually used during trajectory revision.

sections.heading: Representing the global camera pose.
sections.text: When frame I i I_{i} is first stored, its source window has a current global placement T src ⁡ ( i ) T_{\operatorname{src}(i)} . Applying this placement to the frame’s local camera pose gives the global camera pose used to construct its scaffold representation. As described in Sec. 2.1 , we represent camera position and orientation separately and concatenate them into a single scaffold state 𝐠 i \mathbf{g}_{i} . Camera position is first expressed in normalized scene units, with median scene depth equal to one. We use three spatial modules with periods λ 1 = 2.4 , λ 2 = 3.2 , λ 3 = 4.0 . \lambda_{1}=2.4,\qquad\lambda_{2}=3.2,\qquad\lambda_{3}=4.0. For module m m , a position 𝐩 i = ( x i , y i , z i ) \mathbf{p}_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i},z_{i}) is converted to periodic coordinates ϕ m , i = 2 ​ π λ m ​ ( x i , y i , z i ) mod 2 ​ π . \bm{\phi}_{m,i}=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda_{m}}(x_{i},y_{i},z_{i})\bmod 2\pi. Thus, each individual module is periodic: positions separated by λ m \lambda_{m} along an encoded axis produce the same phase in that module. A single periodic module cannot distinguish locations separated by its period. The three modules reduce this ambiguity because their periods are different: a displacement that wraps one module generally does not wrap the other two at the same location. We use ( 2.4 , 3.2 , 4.0 ) = 0.8 ​ ( 3 , 4 , 5 ) , (2.4,3.2,4.0)=0.8(3,4,5), so the complete three-module pattern repeats only after 0.8 ​ lcm ⁡ ( 3 , 4 , 5 ) = 48 0.8\,\operatorname{lcm}(3,4,5)=48 normalized units along an encoded axis. The representation is therefore less ambiguous than any individual module, although it is still periodic rather than globally unique over an unbounded scene. These periods are fixed across the main experiments; we do not claim that they are an optimal set of spatial periods. For each spatial module, the horizontal phase is represented on a 48 × 48 48\times 48 periodic grid and height on a 48-unit ring. These numbers specify the resolution with which a module represents its phase; they are distinct from the spatial period λ m \lambda_{m} . We use 48 × 48 48\times 48 as the default horizontal resolution. The sensitivity study in Table S4 additionally evaluates 16 × 16 16\times 16 and 64 × 64 64\times 64 modules and shows that the method does not depend on using the finest tested resolution.

sections.heading: Representing camera orientation.
sections.text: Camera orientation is converted to yaw, pitch, and roll using the ZYX convention. Each angle is represented on a separate 256-unit periodic ring. A ring is natural for an angular variable because the beginning and end of the interval correspond to the same orientation after a full 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} rotation. The three spatial modules and three orientation rings are concatenated, giving 𝐠 i ∈ ℝ N g , N g = 3 ​ ( 48 2 + 48 ) + 3 ​ ( 256 ) = 7,824 . \mathbf{g}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{g}},\qquad N_{g}=3(48^{2}+48)+3(256)=7{,}824. Thus, 𝐠 i \mathbf{g}_{i} is the scaffold representation of where frame I i I_{i} was estimated to have been captured when it entered memory.

sections.heading: From the scaffold state to a compact memory address.
sections.text: Directly associating visual descriptors with the full 7,824 7{,}824 -dimensional scaffold state would make the associative layer unnecessarily large. We therefore project the scaffold state into a smaller address space: 𝐳 i = W g ​ h ​ 𝐠 i , W g ​ h ∈ ℝ 1024 × 7824 . \mathbf{z}_{i}=W_{gh}\mathbf{g}_{i},\qquad W_{gh}\in\mathbb{R}^{1024\times 7824}. The entries of W g ​ h W_{gh} are sampled independently from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 / 7824 ) \mathcal{N}(0,1/7824) and the matrix remains fixed throughout inference. We then retain only the largest 64 entries: 𝐯 i = σ 64 ​ ( 𝐳 i ) , 𝐡 i = 𝐯 i ‖ 𝐯 i ‖ 2 , \mathbf{v}_{i}=\sigma_{64}(\mathbf{z}_{i}),\qquad\mathbf{h}_{i}=\frac{\mathbf{v}_{i}}{\|\mathbf{v}_{i}\|_{2}}, where σ 64 \sigma_{64} sets all but the 64 largest values to zero. The resulting 𝐡 i ∈ ℝ 1024 \mathbf{h}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{1024} is the memory address of frame I i I_{i} . The purpose of the top- k k operation is to make different addresses selective: unrelated scaffold states activate only a small subset of the 1024 address units, reducing overlap between stored representations. The main configuration retains k = 64 k=64 units, i.e., 6.25 % 6.25\% of the address layer. We use this as a fixed sparsity setting throughout the main experiments. The address dimension is examined in Table S4 : increasing it from the default N h = 1024 N_{h}=1024 to 8192 8192 does not consistently improve the final results, while reducing it to 512 512 produces only a modest change. Thus, the reported gains do not rely on an exceptionally large address layer. Normalizing 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} also makes comparisons between addresses depend on their represented direction and overlap rather than on the absolute magnitude produced by the random projection. The memory address does not contain the RGB frame or its dense geometry. Instead, 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} is linked to the corresponding content-bank entry. That entry stores the RGB frame, its source window, and its camera pose and point map in the local coordinate system of that source window. Appendix C explains how the current global placement T src ⁡ ( i ) T_{\operatorname{src}(i)} is applied when this content is used. The address is assigned when the frame is first stored. Later placement corrections update T src ⁡ ( i ) T_{\operatorname{src}(i)} but do not recompute 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} . This separation allows the stored local geometry to move with its source window without rewriting the content bank or its memory index.

sections.heading: Associating visual content with the same address.
sections.text: The scaffold tells us where a stored frame was captured, but at test time we begin with what the current frame looks like. Therefore, each frame I i I_{i} is independently encoded using the frozen DINOv2 ViT-S/14 encoder ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) . We use its normalized 384-dimensional CLS representation 𝐬 i ∈ ℝ 384 \mathbf{s}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{384} as the frame descriptor. sections.text: The four mappings together form 𝐠 i ⇌ W h ​ g W g ​ h 𝐡 i ⇌ W h ​ s W s ​ h 𝐬 i \boxed{\mathbf{g}_{i}\;\xrightleftharpoons[W_{hg}]{W_{gh}}\;\mathbf{h}_{i}\;\xrightleftharpoons[W_{hs}]{W_{sh}}\;\mathbf{s}_{i}} and connect the spatial and visual information associated with a stored frame. sections.text: For a current frame I q I_{q} , we compute its descriptor 𝐬 q \mathbf{s}_{q} and use only the appearance-to-address direction of the associative memory: 𝐡 ~ q = W s ​ h ​ 𝐬 q ‖ W s ​ h ​ 𝐬 q ‖ 2 + 10 − 12 . \widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{q}=\frac{W_{sh}\mathbf{s}_{q}}{\|W_{sh}\mathbf{s}_{q}\|_{2}+10^{-12}}. We retain at most the five highest-scoring candidates and apply the eligibility conditions from Sec. 2.2 : j < r k − Δ , src ⁡ ( j ) ≠ k − 1 , 𝐬 q ⊤ ​ 𝐬 j ≥ τ app . j<r_{k}-\Delta,\qquad\operatorname{src}(j)\neq k-1,\qquad\mathbf{s}_{q}^{\top}\mathbf{s}_{j}\geq\tau_{\mathrm{app}}. (3) The first condition prevents a temporally nearby frame from being treated as a long-range revisit. The second removes the immediately preceding source window, which is already connected to the current window through their overlap. The third requires the retrieved frame to remain visually compatible with the query. The surviving frames are only candidates; their geometric consistency is checked in Sec. 2.2 and expanded in Appendix F . In particular, we do not decode 𝐡 ~ q \widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{q} through W h ​ g W_{hg} and use the resulting state as the current frame’s global pose. Once a frame is retrieved, its source window identifies its current global placement T src ⁡ ( j ) T_{\operatorname{src}(j)} , while new camera predictions from the geometry foundation model provide the relative transformation used to verify the revisit.

sections.heading: Appendix E Scaffold Dynamics and Controlled Memory Diagnostics
sections.text: The previous section described the scaffold as the mapping 𝐠 ↔ 𝐡 ↔ 𝐬 \mathbf{g}\leftrightarrow\mathbf{h}\leftrightarrow\mathbf{s} used to store and retrieve frames. Here we briefly describe the continuous attractor structure underlying 𝐠 \mathbf{g} and report controlled tests of its behavior. These tests characterize the memory representation itself; they are separate from the end-to-end trajectory experiments.

sections.heading: Continuous attractor fields.
sections.text: Each spatial or orientation component of the scaffold is represented by a periodic neural field, following continuous-attractor models of spatial and directional coding ( Burak and Fiete, 2009 ; Bicanski and Burgess, 2020 ) . The field maintains a localized region of high activation, which we call an activity bump . The position of this bump around a ring or torus represents the encoded coordinate. For example, an orientation ring represents one angular variable such as yaw. Moving the bump around the ring changes the represented angle, while a full revolution returns to the same state. The spatial modules use the same principle on periodic two-dimensional grids and height rings. Thus, the scaffold stores pose through the location of the activity pattern rather than through its overall magnitude.

sections.heading: Maintaining and moving the represented pose.
sections.text: Local excitation together with broader inhibition allows an activity bump to remain stable once formed ( Amari, 1977 ) . A motion input can translate the bump across the periodic field, so changes in camera position or orientation correspond to changes in its phase. Observed camera poses provide anchors for the represented state; the scaffold therefore does not rely only on accumulating motion over time. The main SMoRe pipeline does not use these dynamics as a replacement for the geometry foundation model’s camera predictions. Instead, the predicted global pose provides the state that is encoded when a frame is stored, as described in Sec. 2.1 .

sections.heading: Returning from an address to a valid scaffold state.
sections.text: Appendix D introduced the return mapping W h ​ g W_{hg} from the sparse address 𝐡 \mathbf{h} to the scaffold state 𝐠 \mathbf{g} . For a state 𝐠 \mathbf{g} , one complete scaffold return is Φ ⁡ ( 𝐠 ) = ψ ⁡ ( W h ​ g ​ σ 64 ​ ( W g ​ h ​ 𝐠 ) ) , \Phi(\mathbf{g})=\psi\!\left(W_{hg}\,\sigma_{64}(W_{gh}\mathbf{g})\right), where ψ \psi normalizes the individual spatial and orientation fields. This return mapping is useful because an associative cue need not reproduce every component of the original scaffold state exactly. The return operation encourages the reconstructed representation to remain consistent with the learned scaffold structure. A perturbation that makes different modules mutually inconsistent can therefore be reduced by the return mapping. By contrast, a coherent displacement that moves all modules to another valid pose is itself a valid scaffold state; determining whether such a state corresponds to the correct physical location requires the geometric verification described in Sec. 2.2 . (a) A stationary orientation ring maintains a localized activity bump; the bump centre represents the encoded angle, while the orange dashed lines show the predicted bump boundaries. (b) When angular motion is supplied, the measured bump velocity closely follows the commanded velocity over the tested range. (c) The spatial phases during a closed two-dimensional path return close to their starting point, illustrating path integration in the periodic scaffold coordinates. (d) Associative recall error as the number of stored states increases. The scaffold configuration with the fitted content return map maintains low error through the largest tested load ( P = 160 P=160 ), whereas the Hopfield-style control accumulates larger error. These are controlled memory diagnostics and do not measure end-to-end reconstruction accuracy or establish an unrestricted memory-capacity limit.

sections.heading: What these diagnostics establish.
sections.text: Fig. S1 checks three properties required by the memory design: a pose representation can remain stable, its phase can move continuously with motion, and a stored scaffold state can be recalled through the associative representation over the tested memory load. These experiments support the internal behavior of the scaffold, while the usefulness of scaffold retrieval for SMoRe is evaluated separately by the end-to-end comparison with flat descriptor retrieval in Table S4 .

sections.heading: Appendix F Geometric Verification of Retrieved Revisits
sections.text: Section 2.2 describes how SMoRe verifies the frames returned by the scaffold before changing any window placement. Here we expand that procedure. The key idea is that a retrieved frame is not trusted from appearance alone: it must provide a geometric connection between the current window and a previously placed source window, and a second source window must support a compatible placement.

sections.heading: Forming a retrieved pair.
sections.text: For each retrieved frame I j I_{j} , we select a nearby stored frame I j − 3 I_{j-3} or I j + 3 I_{j+3} . The partner must belong to the same source window as I j I_{j} and satisfy the sequential eligibility rule from Sec. 2.2 . If neither partner frame is valid, the retrieved frame is discarded. The two frames form a retrieved pair . A pair is used instead of a single frame because two camera poses provide a geometric baseline for aligning the new prediction with the stored source window. We use an offset of three frames as a fixed design choice so that the second frame is nearby but distinct.

sections.heading: Why use two different source windows?
sections.text: We retain two retrieved pairs, denoted a a and b b . The two frames within each pair come from the same source window, but the two pairs must come from different source windows. Because every stored frame records its source window, we enforce src ⁡ ( j a ) ≠ src ⁡ ( j b ) . \operatorname{src}(j_{a})\neq\operatorname{src}(j_{b}). This distinction is important. Each source window has its own global placement T T . If both pairs came from the same source window, both placement proposals would depend on the same historical reference. Using two different source windows instead provides two separately placed references with which to check the current window. We use two pairs by default. One pair provides no second historical placement with which to test agreement, while a third pair requires two additional frames. Table S4 compares one, two, and three pairs and shows that two retain most of the measured benefit of three with fewer additional inputs.

sections.heading: Joint prediction with the current window.
sections.text: If two valid pairs are available, the frozen geometry foundation model processes the 32 current-window frames together with the four retrieved frames, giving 36 input frames in total. The 32 current frames retain their sequential order, and the four retrieved frames are appended as the two pairs. Because all 36 frames are processed together, their camera poses are predicted in one common local coordinate system. This joint prediction creates a direct geometric relationship between the current window and the retrieved historical frames; the existing chain of window placements is not used to create that relationship.

sections.heading: Obtaining a global-placement proposal.
sections.text: Consider retrieved pair a a , whose source window is 𝒲 o a \mathcal{W}_{o_{a}} . The two frames in this pair have camera poses from the new joint prediction and stored camera poses in the local coordinate system of 𝒲 o a \mathcal{W}_{o_{a}} . Using the similarity-alignment procedure from Appendix B , we align these two sets of camera poses and obtain Z ^ o a , k , \widehat{Z}_{o_{a},k}, the measured transformation relating the current joint prediction to source window 𝒲 o a \mathcal{W}_{o_{a}} . Since 𝒲 o a \mathcal{W}_{o_{a}} already has the global placement T o a T_{o_{a}} , pair a a proposes the current window placement T k ( a ) = T o a ​ Z ^ o a , k . T_{k}^{(a)}=T_{o_{a}}\widehat{Z}_{o_{a},k}. Repeating exactly the same procedure for pair b b gives T k ( b ) = T o b ​ Z ^ o b , k . T_{k}^{(b)}=T_{o_{b}}\widehat{Z}_{o_{b},k}. Thus, the two retrieved pairs independently of the retrieval score provide two geometric proposals for where the current window should lie in the global reconstruction. The scaffold is used to find the historical frames; the geometry foundation model and their stored source-window placements determine these proposals.

sections.heading: Checking whether the two proposals agree.
sections.text: We accept the revisit only if T k ( a ) T_{k}^{(a)} and T k ( b ) T_{k}^{(b)} place the current window sufficiently close to one another. Let E k E_{k} denote the median distance of the current-window camera positions from their mean position after global placement. We use this quantity to scale the translation tolerance to the size of the current reconstruction. The two proposals must satisfy ∠ ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( T k ( a ) ) , R ⁡ ( T k ( b ) ) ) ≤ 10 ∘ , ‖ c ⁡ ( T k ( a ) ) − c ⁡ ( T k ( b ) ) ‖ 2 ≤ E k . \angle\!\left(R(T_{k}^{(a)}),R(T_{k}^{(b)})\right)\leq 10^{\circ},\qquad\left\|c(T_{k}^{(a)})-c(T_{k}^{(b)})\right\|_{2}\leq E_{k}. (4) The first condition checks rotational agreement, while the second checks translation relative to the scale of the scene. If either condition fails, the retrieved frames are rejected and no retrieval-based placement correction is applied. If both conditions pass, the revisit is accepted and the resulting geometric constraint is used to revise the window placements, as described in Appendix G .

sections.heading: What verification does and does not guarantee.
sections.text: The two source windows provide two separate geometric checks, but this does not guarantee that every accepted revisit is correct. Repeated scene structure, inaccurate historical placements, or weak two-camera geometry can still produce compatible but incorrect proposals. The agreement test therefore acts as a practical consistency check rather than a proof of correspondence. Jointly processing the retrieved frames can also change the current window’s local camera poses and point maps before the agreement decision is made. Rejecting a revisit prevents the global placement correction, but does not automatically restore the prediction obtained from the current window alone. We examine this separate effect in Appendix M . Our default configuration therefore retains the joint prediction only when it stays within 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} of the prediction from the current window alone.

sections.heading: Appendix G Trajectory Revision and Global Refinement
sections.text: Section 2.2 describes the online correction applied after a revisit has been verified, while we also do the final refinement after the full sequence has been processed. Both operations modify the global window placements T k T_{k} ; the camera poses and point maps stored inside each source window remain in their local coordinate systems, as explained in Appendix C .

sections.text: Only the global placements T ℓ T_{\ell} are modified. The camera poses and point maps stored for frames in 𝒲 ℓ \mathcal{W}_{\ell} remain unchanged in their source-window coordinates. Applying the updated T ℓ T_{\ell} therefore moves the cameras and their associated 3D geometry together. Therefore, a correction made at one revisit can influence the global placements used when subsequent frames are stored and when later revisits are verified.

sections.heading: Recording constraints between windows.
sections.text: In addition to updating the running trajectory, SMoRe retains the relative geometric measurements obtained while processing the sequence. There are two types of connections. A sequential connection is obtained from the shared frames of two neighboring windows. A revisit connection is obtained from an accepted historical retrieval. For a connection e = ( ℓ , k ) e=(\ell,k) , let Z e Z_{e} denote the measured relative transformation between windows 𝒲 ℓ \mathcal{W}_{\ell} and 𝒲 k \mathcal{W}_{k} . sections.heading: Final global refinement.
sections.text: Online corrections are applied one revisit at a time. After all windows have been processed, SMoRe jointly refines the complete set of window placements using all retained sequential and accepted revisit connections. We fix T 1 T_{1} to remove the global gauge freedom and optimize min ⁡ ∑ e = ( ℓ , k ) ∈ ℰ T 2 , … , T K ⁡ ρ H ​ ( ‖ Log ⁡ ( Z e − 1 ​ T ℓ − 1 ​ T k ) ‖ Λ e 2 ) , \min_{T_{2},\ldots,T_{K}}\sum_{e=(\ell,k)\in\mathcal{E}}\rho_{H}\!\left(\left\|\operatorname{Log}\left(Z_{e}^{-1}T_{\ell}^{-1}T_{k}\right)\right\|_{\Lambda_{e}}^{2}\right), (8) where ℰ \mathcal{E} is the set of retained connections. The quantity Z e − 1 ​ T ℓ − 1 ​ T k Z_{e}^{-1}T_{\ell}^{-1}T_{k} measures the disagreement between the relative placement predicted by the current trajectory and the relative transformation measured from the frames. Taking Log \operatorname{Log} converts this disagreement into rotation, translation, and scale components that can be optimized together. The diagonal matrix Λ e \Lambda_{e} controls the relative contribution of these components, while the Huber loss ρ H \rho_{H} ( Huber, 1964 ) reduces the influence of unusually large residuals. This is a pose-graph optimization over window placements rather than bundle adjustment over individual 3D points ( Grisetti et al., 2010 ; Kümmerle et al., 2011 ; Dellaert, 2012 ) .

sections.heading: Handling inconsistent revisit constraints.
sections.text: An accepted revisit can still be incorrect, for example, because of repeated scene structure. We therefore perform the global solve robustly. After the first optimization, revisit connections with large residuals are rejected according to the configured residual criterion, and the remaining graph is optimized once more. Sequential connections are retained because they define the basic chain of the reconstruction.

sections.heading: Online revision versus final refinement.
sections.text: The two stages serve different purposes. The distributed update in Eq. 7 corrects the trajectory while the sequence is still being processed, so later observations benefit from the revised placements. The optimization in Eq. 8 instead considers all measurements together after the sequence is complete and removes remaining global inconsistencies. Both stages update only the window placements.

sections.heading: H.1 Camera Pose Estimation
sections.text: The camera-pose experiments in Sec. 3.1 evaluate how pose accuracy changes as more frames from the same video trajectory are processed. We use CO3Dv2 and RealEstate10K because they provide different camera-motion patterns: CO3Dv2 contains object-centric trajectories with substantial viewpoint changes, whereas RE10K is dominated by forward camera motion and therefore contains fewer natural revisits.

sections.heading: CO3Dv2.
sections.text: We use 37 CO3Dv2 sequences with validated camera trajectories. The videos span approximately 8–68 s, with a median duration of 26 s. For each trajectory, we evaluate N ∈ { 10 , 50 , 100 , 200 } N\in\{10,50,100,200\} input frames. Frames are sampled uniformly across the available trajectory rather than taking the first N N frames. Thus, increasing N N increases the temporal density with which the same underlying trajectory is observed. The controlled pose ablations in Appendix J use a separate subset of twelve CO3Dv2 trajectories at N = 200 N=200 and should not be interpreted as the full 37-sequence evaluation.

sections.heading: RealEstate10K.
sections.text: RE10K contains real-estate videos with predominantly forward camera motion ( Zhou et al., 2018 ) . The 100 clips used for the length study span 6.7–9.3 s, with a median duration of 9.3 s. We uniformly sample N ∈ { 50,100,200 } N\in\{50,100,200\} frames from these clips. For the N = 10 N=10 evaluation, we use the larger set of 1,653 usable test clips. The N = 10 N=10 and longer-sequence evaluations therefore use different numbers of clips and should not be interpreted as a nested set of the same sequences.

sections.heading: Pose metric.
sections.text: Following the relative-pose evaluation used in the main experiments, we evaluate every pair of sampled frames. For a pair ( i , j ) (i,j) , we compute its rotation error and translation-direction error and define the pairwise pose error as e i ​ j = max ⁡ ( e i ​ j rot , e i ​ j trans ) . e_{ij}=\max\left(e_{ij}^{\mathrm{rot}},e_{ij}^{\mathrm{trans}}\right). Translation magnitude is not scored because monocular geometry is defined only up to scale. AUC@30 is the normalized area under the cumulative distribution of e i ​ j e_{ij} between 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} and 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} . Higher AUC therefore means that a larger fraction of frame pairs have accurate relative camera poses. Table S2 reports the mean and standard deviation over the evaluated sequences or clips.

sections.heading: H.2 Multi-view Depth Estimation and 3D Point-Cloud Reconstruction
sections.text: The experiments in Sec. 3.2 evaluate multi-view depth estimation on Replica ( Straub et al., 2019 ) and 3D point-cloud reconstruction on ScanNet++ ( Yeshwanth et al., 2023 ) . Both are evaluated in the same long-horizon setting using 32-frame windows with 16-frame overlap, as described in Sec. 2 . Each window is first reconstructed locally by the frozen geometry foundation model and then placed in the shared global coordinate system using the overlapping frames. Baseline and + SMoRe +\textsc{SMoRe}{} use exactly the same input frames, windowing strategy, and geometry foundation model. Baseline connects the windows sequentially without long-range memory, whereas + SMoRe +\textsc{SMoRe}{} additionally retrieves earlier observations, verifies candidate revisits, and uses accepted geometric evidence to revise the global placements of the reconstructed windows.

sections.heading: Replica.
sections.text: Replica ( Straub et al., 2019 ) provides photorealistic synthetic indoor environments together with accurate camera information and dense reference 3D geometry. It contains 18 such scenes with about 2000 frames per scene. Its controlled geometry allows us to measure how reconstruction errors accumulate as a scene is processed across many overlapping windows. For each evaluated trajectory, Baseline and + SMoRe +\textsc{SMoRe}{} process the same frames in the same temporal order; the only difference is whether the external memory is used to retrieve and revise previously placed reconstruction windows.

sections.heading: ScanNet++.
sections.text: ScanNet++ ( Yeshwanth et al., 2023 ) contains high-resolution observations of real indoor environments together with high-quality reference 3D geometry. It contains 1006 scenes with about 8000 frames per scene. Compared with Replica, it evaluates the same long-horizon reconstruction procedure under real image appearance, camera motion, and more complex scene geometry. We again use identical input frames and 32-frame windows for Baseline and + SMoRe +\textsc{SMoRe}{} , so improvements measure the effect of memory-based revisit verification and trajectory revision rather than differences in the input data or geometry foundation model.

sections.heading: Dense-geometry metrics.
sections.text: For both datasets, we report accuracy , completeness , and overall reconstruction error. Accuracy measures the distance from the reconstructed geometry to the reference geometry, while completeness measures the reverse distance from the reference geometry to the reconstruction. We define the overall error as the mean of accuracy and completeness. All distances are reported in centimetres, and lower values indicate better reconstruction. Table 1 reports the mean and standard deviation over the corresponding evaluation set.

sections.heading: Appendix I Novel View Synthesis Protocol and Decoder
sections.text: We evaluate whether revising stored geometry improves novel view synthesis from long sequences. We use the same frozen geometry models, windowing scheme, and memory configuration as in the camera pose experiments. A Gaussian decoder converts the stored geometry into rendered images. The datasets and evaluation splits are described in Appendix H.5 .

sections.heading: I.1 Source Views and Geometry
sections.text: We render each held-out target from eight nearby input keyframes. Source views are selected using the sum of camera-centre distance and viewing-direction angle, computed from the ground-truth cameras. The target itself is excluded. Baseline and + SMoRe +\textsc{SMoRe}{} use identical source views. Each source keyframe retains the depth, confidence, and camera intrinsics predicted when it first enters a window. Its depth is unprojected into 3D points in that window’s local coordinate system (Appendix C ). Baseline places these points in the global map using chained window transformations T k T_{k} . SMoRe uses the window transformations obtained after online revision. We fit a similarity transformation between the estimated and ground-truth input cameras. We use this alignment to express the target camera in each map’s coordinate system. Before decoding, we centre the source points at the centre of the source cameras and normalize their scale by the median source depth. We discard the lowest-confidence 30% of points in each frame. We also remove points at depth discontinuities, defined by a relative depth difference above 5% between neighbouring pixels. Both systems use the same filtering procedure. Images are rendered at 384 × 288 384\times 288 resolution with a 4:3 aspect ratio. Portrait CO3Dv2 sequences retain their original orientation.

sections.heading: I.2 Gaussian Decoder and Training
sections.text: We use a Gaussian decoder to predict rendering parameters from the source images and their geometry. Each source pixel provides eleven input channels: 3 ⏟ RGB + 3 ⏟ map position + 1 ⏟ depth + 1 ⏟ log-confidence + 3 ⏟ ray direction = 11 . \underbrace{3}_{\text{RGB}}+\underbrace{3}_{\text{map position}}+\underbrace{1}_{\text{depth}}+\underbrace{1}_{\text{log-confidence}}+\underbrace{3}_{\text{ray direction}}=11. A four-level U-Net with approximately 7M parameters predicts a position offset, log-scales, rotation, opacity, and colour residual for each valid pixel. The position offset is bounded by two pixel footprints, and the scales are predicted relative to the footprint. A pixel’s footprint is its depth multiplied by the pixel size and divided by the focal length. This parameterization scales the Gaussians according to the input geometry. The Gaussians from all source views are rasterized into the target view using gsplat ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) . An image-space U-Net with approximately 3M parameters then refines the rendering. It takes the rendered colour, alpha, and depth as input and predicts a bounded colour residual. The decoder is initialized to approximate splatting the coloured source points.

sections.heading: Training data.
sections.text: For each geometry model, we train one decoder on the chained geometry and another on the geometry maintained by SMoRe . Both decoders use the same architecture, training data, schedule, and random seed. Training uses all 7-Scenes sequences except seq-01. These sequences are processed with the same windowing and memory configuration as the test sequences, and every keyframe is stored. Each training sample consists of one target keyframe and its eight nearest source keyframes. We exclude the target and its immediate neighbours from the source set, so the target image does not provide source pixels.

sections.heading: Optimization.
sections.text: We train the decoders with an image reconstruction loss: ℒ = ℒ 1 + 0.5 ​ ℒ LPIPS + 0.2 ​ ( 1 − SSIM ) . \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{1}+0.5\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LPIPS}}+0.2\,(1-\mathrm{SSIM}). We use AdamW for 12K steps with a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , 500 warm-up steps, and cosine decay. Gradients are accumulated over two samples. Training takes approximately one hour per decoder on an RTX 6000 Ada GPU. Neither the geometry foundation model nor SMoRe is optimized by this loss. The comparison therefore evaluates each geometry representation with its own trained decoder under matched training conditions.

sections.heading: I.3 Evaluation and Additional Results
sections.text: We render each held-out target from the chained map with the Baseline decoder and from the revised map with the + SMoRe +\textsc{SMoRe}{} decoder. We compute PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS against the target image, following Appendix H.5 . Gains are computed from paired differences between the two renderings of each target. Figure S3 reports the paired PSNR gains on 7-Scenes and their standard errors. Decoders trained on 7-Scenes are evaluated on CO3Dv2 without adaptation, testing transfer from indoor scenes to object-centric sequences.

sections.heading: Results on revisited regions.
sections.text: On 7-Scenes, the mean paired PSNR gains range from 0.31 to 0.71 dB across the six geometry models, with standard errors of 0.10 to 0.13 dB. All six 95% confidence intervals exclude zero. Revisited targets show larger gains. For example, VGGT- Ω \Omega and STream3R improve by 1.00 and 1.14 dB on revisited targets, compared with 0.53 and 0.71 dB over all targets. These results are consistent with the role of window revision in aligning repeated observations of the same surfaces. On CO3Dv2, STream3R accepts few revisits along the object-centric trajectories and shows little change in PSNR. Fast3R improves SSIM and LPIPS but decreases PSNR by 0.12 dB.

sections.heading: Reference window placement.
sections.text: We also evaluate a reference placement obtained by fitting each stored window’s local cameras to the ground-truth cameras with a similarity transformation. We render these windows with the + SMoRe +\textsc{SMoRe}{} decoder. This reference is not an upper bound, since camera alignment does not ensure consistency between the local geometry of different windows. For π 3 \pi^{3} on 7-Scenes, the reference achieves 16.43 dB, below the Baseline result of 17.24 dB. For the other five models, it exceeds + SMoRe +\textsc{SMoRe}{} by 0.2 to 1.0 dB on both datasets. Thus, the effect of window placement also depends on the consistency of the predicted local geometry. Figure S3: Gaussian decoder training and novel view synthesis results. sections.heading: Appendix J Controlled Ablations
sections.text: We expand the model analysis of Sec. 3.5 in the same order as the main text. We first test whether the scaffold improves retrieval over direct descriptor matching, and then vary the visual descriptor used to query the scaffold. We next examine how much historical evidence is needed to verify a revisit and whether an accepted revisit must revise the trajectory online. Finally, we study sensitivity to the scaffold and window configurations. We report ATE (m) on 7-Scenes ( Shotton et al., 2013 ) and AUC@30 on CO3Dv2 ( Reizenstein et al., 2021 ) in these ablations.

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: Unless stated otherwise, the pose ablations use seven 7-Scenes seq-01 trajectories with 200 frames and VGGT- Ω \Omega ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , together with twelve 200-frame CO3Dv2 trajectories and VGGT ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . Paired variants use the same input frames. The common raw references are 0.045 m ATE on 7-Scenes and 88.8 AUC@30 on CO3D. We use Online for the trajectory available during sequence processing and Final for the result after the final global refinement. Lower ATE is better, whereas higher AUC@30 is better.
