sections.heading: J.2 Which Visual Descriptor Should Query the Scaffold?
sections.text: We next keep the scaffold and the downstream revision procedure fixed and change the visual descriptor used to retrieve stored frames (Table S4 , Group C). We compare the default DINOv2 CLS descriptor ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) with NetVLAD ( Arandjelovic et al., 2016 ) , EigenPlaces ( Berton et al., 2023 ) , CosPlace ( Berton et al., 2022 ) , MixVPR ( Ali-Bey et al., 2023 ) , SALAD ( Izquierdo and Civera, 2024 ) , and BoQ ( Ali-Bey et al., 2024 ) , together with two concatenated descriptors. The production DINOv2 configuration uses its fixed 0.5 appearance gate. The alternative descriptors are evaluated without descriptor-specific gates so that a separate threshold is not tuned for each method. The top-five retrieval budget, geometric verification, online revision, and final refinement remain unchanged. None of the tested alternatives improves over the production DINOv2 configuration on the final reconstruction. This result also shows that retrieving visually plausible frames is not sufficient by itself: the retrieved frames must provide useful geometric evidence for the subsequent verification and trajectory revision. Appendix M separately examines how changing the retrieved historical frames can affect the current window’s local prediction before verification.

sections.heading: J.3 How Much Historical Evidence Is Needed?
sections.text: Section 2.2 uses two retrieved pairs from different source windows to verify a revisit. In Table S4 (Group E), we first vary the number of retrieved pairs while keeping the rest of the pipeline unchanged. We then disable the online placement update to distinguish verifying a revisit from actually using it to revise the trajectory. Using only one retrieved pair substantially degrades 7-Scenes ATE, whereas three pairs give similar online performance to two on both benchmarks. Three pairs keep the 7-Scenes ATE to 0.029. We therefore use two pairs as the default evidence. The online placement update is also important. When revisits are proposed and verified but not applied online, 7-Scenes ATE increases from 0.030 to 0.042 m and CO3Dv2 AUC@30 decreases from 93.4 to 91.3. The final global refinement can recover part of this loss, but those corrections are unavailable while later windows are being processed. The no-update row remains different from the raw trajectory because the default configuration retains the joint-pass local predictions; this effect is isolated in Appendix M . The additional rows test how accepted measurements are applied. The default online update re-solves the affected local pose graph using the accepted revisit measurement and the sequential constraints. The Distributed correction row instead applies the direct interpolation of the measured correction across the affected windows. Removing outlier rejection from the final global solve mainly reduces the final CO3Dv2 score, while separately re-measuring the historical frames changes the reported accuracy only modestly.

sections.heading: J.4 Sensitivity to Scaffold and Window Size
sections.text: We next vary the dimensions of the scaffold representation and the window used by the geometry foundation model in Table S4 (Group D). These experiments test sensitivity rather than removing a component: changing these quantities also changes the memory resolution or the input context available to the geometry foundation model. Performance is relatively stable across the tested scaffold dimensions. Increasing the address dimension from 1024 to 8192 does not consistently improve the final result, and increasing the torus resolution to 64 2 64^{2} can reduce accuracy. Therefore, it shows that the memory structure itself is good at recall, and increasing the dimensionality of the address does not necessarily show us gains. On the other hand (Group B), optimal sparsity σ = 64 \sigma=64 is set so that sparse addresses are near orthogonal to each other with minimum overlap, while too much sparsity results in loss of information. Window size has a stronger effect because it changes both the geometry predictions and the number of junctions between windows. We observe that the performance over both 7-scenes and CO3Dv2 improves with larger window size and moderate overlap ratio. As the overlap ratio increases, the number of windows increases, and so does the chaining error evident in Table S4 . Also observe that a smaller window size increases the number of windows too, which is why we see degraded performance for W = 16 W=16 . Since the gains are so marginal, we select the best window size and overlap ratio with a simple grid search over these two parameters.

sections.heading: Summary.
sections.text: Together, these ablations support the main design choices used by SMoRe : scaffold-based retrieval improves over direct descriptor matching, DINOv2 provides the strongest tested retrieval cue, two retrieved pairs provide an effective verification budget, and applying accepted revisit measurements online substantially improves the running trajectory. The scaffold dimensions, window size, and activation sparsity of the scaffold address were all tuned to maximize performance across all tasks.

sections.heading: Appendix K Compute and Memory Measurements
sections.text: We examine how SMoRe changes the computational and memory requirements of geometry foundation models as sequences become longer. For feed-forward models, long sequences are processed as overlapping windows whose local reconstructions must be connected across the trajectory, while streaming models retain causal context from earlier frames inside the model. In contrast, SMoRe keeps geometry-model inference bounded to the current window and stores long-horizon information in its external memory. Earlier observations are brought back into the geometry foundation model only when they are retrieved for revisit verification. All measurements use one RTX 6000 Ada GPU with a tested 46 GB GPU-memory budget, batch size one, and public model weights. We use the CO3Dv2 camera-pose experiment from Sec. 3.1 . The default SMoRe configuration uses 32-frame windows; during revisit verification, up to four retrieved historical frames can be processed together with the current window, giving at most 36 frames in one geometry-model invocation.

sections.heading: K.1 Peak GPU Memory with Increasing Sequence Length
sections.text: We first study peak GPU allocation as the number of input frames increases from N = 10 N=10 to N = 200 N=200 . Table S5 shows how the bounded-window design of SMoRe limits the GPU working set over longer sequences. For feed-forward models, the sequence is reconstructed using overlapping windows and the resulting local predictions are chained through their shared frames. As the sequence grows, the baseline can retain increasing amounts of intermediate predictions and geometric information needed to connect these windows. With SMoRe , the geometry foundation model still operates on a bounded current window, while earlier observations are stored in the external scaffold and content bank and are selectively reintroduced only when needed. For example, VGGT grows from 9.1 GB at N = 10 N=10 to 23.9 GB at N = 200 N=200 in the baseline, whereas SMoRe remains between 8.5 and 9.6 GB. VGGT- Ω \Omega similarly grows from 5.7 to 19.5 GB in the baseline but remains near 7 GB with SMoRe . Streaming models exhibit a different source of GPU-memory growth. Their native causal inference retains internal states or cached tokens from previous frames so that earlier observations can influence later predictions. These GPU-resident states grow with the sequence. StreamVGGT therefore increases from 8.6 GB at N = 10 N=10 to 22.7 GB at N = 100 N=100 and exceeds the tested 46 GB budget at N = 200 N=200 . STream3R exceeds the same budget from N = 50 N=50 onward. With SMoRe , long-range information is instead maintained externally and the geometry model receives bounded windows plus only a small number of retrieved frames. StreamVGGT therefore uses 11.4 GB at N = 200 N=200 , while STream3R remains feasible at 25.4 GB. The total memory used by SMoRe is not constant: the content bank grows as additional observations are stored. The important distinction is that this history does not remain part of the geometry foundation model’s active GPU context. Consequently, peak GPU allocation is governed mainly by the bounded model invocation rather than by the complete trajectory. sections.heading: K.2 Compute and Runtime at N = 100 N=100
sections.text: Reducing peak GPU memory does not make SMoRe computationally free. Instead, SMoRe trades a bounded GPU working set for additional operations required to maintain and verify its external memory. Table S6 measures this trade-off at N = 100 N=100 and reports accumulated CPU processing time, peak host RAM, peak GPU allocation, total floating-point computation, and end-to-end wall-clock runtime. CPU time is accumulated across host processing and can therefore differ from the wall-clock runtime, while RAM reports the peak resident host-memory footprint. The additional computation comes from three main sources. First, incoming frames require visual-descriptor extraction, scaffold lookup, and content-bank operations. Second, when a candidate revisit is retrieved, the historical frames are processed jointly with the current window so that their geometric relationship can be re-estimated. Third, accepted revisits require similarity alignment and trajectory revision. These operations increase CPU processing and can add geometry-model forward passes, explaining the higher CPU time and PFLOP count for SMoRe . The external memory also introduces a modest host-RAM cost. For most models, this increase is small at N = 100 N=100 : VGGT changes from 10.77 to 10.78 GB, VGGT- Ω \Omega from 9.88 to 9.89 GB, π 3 \pi^{3} from 11.58 to 11.59 GB, DUSt3R from 16.94 to 17.02 GB, and MASt3R from 17.23 to 17.29 GB. StreamVGGT increases from 10.45 to 10.79 GB, while Fast3R shows the largest increase, from 7.42 to 8.60 GB. This reflects the intended resource trade-off: persistent observations and memory metadata are maintained outside the geometry model, allowing the GPU-resident working set to remain bounded. Peak GPU allocation and total computation should therefore be interpreted separately. SMoRe may execute more total operations while still using less peak GPU memory because additional verification passes are performed sequentially on bounded inputs. For example, VGGT increases from 2.20 to 2.44 PFLOP and from 0.33 to 0.54 min runtime, while its peak GPU allocation decreases from 15.1 to 9.6 GB. VGGT- Ω \Omega increases from 1.08 to 1.26 PFLOP while reducing GPU allocation from 11.9 to 6.9 GB, and π 3 \pi^{3} reduces GPU allocation from 26.5 to 14.1 GB despite increasing from 1.52 to 1.82 PFLOP. Finally, wall-clock runtime is dominated by the cost of the underlying geometry foundation model. The same SMoRe memory operations are applied across models, yet + SMoRe +\textsc{SMoRe}{} requires only 0.38 min for VGGT- Ω \Omega and 0.42 min for Fast3R, compared with 17.01 min for DUSt3R and 18.49 min for MASt3R. Thus, the absolute runtime cost is determined primarily by the geometry-model inference required during ordinary processing and revisit verification rather than by the scaffold itself. sections.heading: Frozen and updated components.
sections.text: All geometry foundation models use their public pretrained weights and remain frozen throughout SMoRe . The DINOv2 encoder used for retrieval is also frozen. The fixed projection W g ​ h W_{gh} is sampled once, while W h ​ g W_{hg} is fitted once before inference from sampled scaffold states. Only the appearance–address associations W s ​ h W_{sh} and W h ​ s W_{hs} are updated online as new frames are stored, using the RLS update in Eq. 2 . Thus, trajectory improvement does not result from fine-tuning the geometry foundation model. The novel-view-synthesis decoders are the only separately trained task-specific components. As described in Appendix I , two decoders of identical architecture, data, schedule, and seed are trained per geometry model, one on its chained geometry and one on the geometry maintained by SMoRe ; neither the geometry model nor SMoRe is trained.

sections.heading: Task-specific protocol differences.
sections.text: The settings in Table S7 describe the default trajectory configuration rather than a requirement that every downstream task use the same window structure. The camera-pose and SLAM experiments use the windowing protocol specified in their respective evaluation sections. The compute study in Appendix K measures ordinary 32-frame passes and joint passes containing up to four additional retrieved frames. Replica and ScanNet++ use the default 32-frame windows with 16-frame overlap and online revisit-driven trajectory revision. Novel view synthesis uses the same windowing and online revision on 7-Scenes and CO3Dv2 trajectories with every eighth keyframe held out, without final global refinement.

sections.heading: Frame selection and dataset subsets.
sections.text: Window size should not be confused with the number of frames evaluated from a complete sequence. The exact dataset subsets and frame-selection rules are specified in Appendix H . In particular, paired Baseline + SMoRe +\textsc{SMoRe}{} comparisons use the same selected frames and the same geometry foundation model. This ensures that changes in the reported metrics are attributable to the corresponding SMoRe procedure rather than to different inputs.

sections.heading: Appendix M Separating Local-Prediction Changes from Trajectory Revision
sections.text: The joint policy retains the current-window prediction produced by joint processing with the retrieved historical frames; it corresponds to the anchored configuration in the diagnostic logs. The ordinary policy retains the prediction of the current window alone. The gated policy, which our default configuration uses with τ dist = 5 ∘ \tau_{\mathrm{dist}}=5^{\circ} , switches between them according to the measured distortion. This section separates these effects. We first define the ordinary and joint passes used by the diagnostic, then compare three policies for deciding which local prediction is retained. We finally test these policies under the default retrieval proposals and under several failure cases.

sections.heading: Evaluation setting.
sections.text: The diagnostics use seven 7-Scenes trajectories with VGGT- Ω \Omega and twelve CO3Dv2 trajectories with VGGT, reusing the cached predictions from the controlled pose study. The raw references are 0.045 m ATE on 7-Scenes and 88.8 AUC@30 on CO3D. Because the purpose of this analysis is to isolate what happens during sequence processing, the tables below report the online trajectory before the final global refinement. Lower ATE is better and higher AUC@30 is better. The main pose experiments retain the current-window prediction produced by joint processing with the retrieved historical frames. We refer to this as the joint policy below; it corresponds to the anchored configuration used in the diagnostic logs. The ordinary and gated policies are diagnostic variants and do not replace the configuration used for the main results.

sections.heading: M.1 Why Rejecting a Revisit Does Not Restore the Original Prediction
sections.text: An ordinary pass processes the 32 frames of the current window alone. When two retrieved pairs are available, the joint pass instead processes those same 32 current frames together with the four retrieved historical frames. The purpose of the joint pass is to place the current and historical frames in one common local coordinate system so that the revisit can be verified. However, the joint pass also produces a new prediction for the current window itself. Under the default policy, this joint prediction becomes the current window’s retained local camera poses and point maps. The subsequent revisit test therefore controls only whether a retrieval-based global placement update is applied. If the revisit is rejected, its placement correction is discarded, but the retained joint-pass local prediction is not replaced by the prediction from the ordinary pass. Consequently, a rejected historical proposal can still influence later windows through the sequential overlap alignment. This is why revisit verification and local-prediction stability must be analyzed separately.

sections.heading: Measuring the change in the local prediction.
sections.text: To measure how much the historical frames change the current-window prediction, we align the camera predictions of the current frames from the joint pass with those from the ordinary pass. After this alignment, the logged quantity ϵ k rot \epsilon_{k}^{\mathrm{rot}} measures the remaining rotational disagreement for window k k , in degrees. This quantity measures agreement between two model predictions; it is not an error against ground truth. A small ϵ k rot \epsilon_{k}^{\mathrm{rot}} means that the joint pass remains close to the ordinary prediction, while a large value indicates that adding the historical frames substantially changed the predicted local camera geometry. For the 50 joint-pass windows in the default seed-0 7-Scenes diagnostic, the median residual is 0.117 ∘ 0.117^{\circ} and the maximum is 0.311 ∘ 0.311^{\circ} . In a separate seed-1 run, however, one chess window reaches 46.1 ∘ 46.1^{\circ} . For that sequence, ATE increases from 0.025 to 0.459 m even though both tested revisit proposals are rejected. Thus, a large local-prediction change can affect the trajectory without an accepted false revisit.

sections.heading: M.2 Three Ways to Retain the Current-Window Prediction
sections.text: We compare three policies that differ only in which current-window local prediction is retained after the joint pass. The joint pass is still available for historical re-measurement in all three cases. Table S8: Local-prediction policies used in the diagnostic. All three policies can use the joint pass to measure the historical relationship. They differ only in which prediction is retained for the current window before sequential placement and possible trajectory revision. Policy Retained current-window prediction Role of the joint pass Joint (default) Prediction from current + + historical frames Provides both the retained local prediction and the revisit measurement Ordinary Prediction from the current window alone Used only to measure the historical relationship Gated Joint prediction if its distortion is small; otherwise ordinary Provides the revisit measurement and a candidate local prediction

sections.heading: Joint policy.
sections.text: The current-window camera poses and point maps are taken directly from the joint pass. This allows the historical frames to influence the local prediction, which can be useful when the retrieved evidence is correct, but also exposes the current prediction to an incorrect proposal before verification.

sections.heading: Ordinary policy.
sections.text: The current window retains the prediction obtained from its ordinary pass. The joint pass is used only to measure the relationship between the historical frames and the current window. The historical predictions from the joint pass are transformed into the retained ordinary coordinate system before verification. Thus, rejecting the revisit leaves the current window with exactly the local prediction it would have had without the historical frames.

sections.heading: Gated policy.
sections.text: The gated policy selects between the two predictions according to their measured rotational disagreement: 𝒫 k sel = { 𝒫 k joint , ϵ k rot ≤ τ dist , 𝒫 k ord , ϵ k rot > τ dist , \mathcal{P}_{k}^{\mathrm{sel}}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{P}_{k}^{\mathrm{joint}},&\epsilon_{k}^{\mathrm{rot}}\leq\tau_{\mathrm{dist}},\\ \mathcal{P}_{k}^{\mathrm{ord}},&\epsilon_{k}^{\mathrm{rot}}>\tau_{\mathrm{dist}},\end{cases} (9) where 𝒫 k joint \mathcal{P}_{k}^{\mathrm{joint}} and 𝒫 k ord \mathcal{P}_{k}^{\mathrm{ord}} denote the current-window predictions from the joint and ordinary passes, respectively, and τ dist \tau_{\mathrm{dist}} is the angular threshold. This gate is applied before the revisit decision. Passing the gate does not mean that the revisit has been accepted; geometric verification in Appendix F is still required. The gate controls which local prediction is retained, whereas revisit verification controls whether a global placement measurement is accepted.

sections.heading: M.3 Does the Local Prediction Matter Without a Placement Update?
sections.text: A direct control is obtained by disabling the online placement update. With the ordinary policy and the update disabled, the resulting trajectory matches the raw trajectory on all seven tested 7-Scenes sequences. With the joint policy and the same update disabled, mean ATE changes from 0.0451 to 0.0423 m. The only difference between these two controls is therefore whether the current window retains the ordinary or joint-pass local prediction. This confirms that joint processing can change the trajectory even when no accepted revisit is written back to the global placements. The seed-1 chess failure above demonstrates the same mechanism in the opposite direction: a large joint-pass distortion can strongly degrade the trajectory even when both proposed revisits are rejected. Together, these controls show that local re-prediction and explicit trajectory revision are separate effects.

sections.heading: M.4 How Much Joint-Pass Distortion Should Be Retained?
sections.text: We first vary the distortion threshold using the default DINOv2 retrieval proposals and scaffold seed 0. Table S9 reports only the online trajectory so that the comparison isolates local-prediction selection from the final global refinement. This is consistent with the seed-0 diagnostic above: the largest measured distortion is only 0.311 ∘ 0.311^{\circ} , so every tested gate with threshold at least 0.5 ∘ 0.5^{\circ} retains the joint prediction for those measured windows. CO3Dv2 shows a clearer trade-off. Always retaining the ordinary prediction gives 92.4 AUC@30, compared with 93.4 for the default joint policy. Thus, suppressing every change introduced by historical frames is not necessarily desirable: some joint-pass changes are useful. The diagnostic instead asks whether large changes can be rejected without discarding all of the benefit of joint processing.

sections.text: The previous experiment uses the default seed and retrieval proposals, for which the measured 7-Scenes distortions are small. We therefore separately examine settings in which the joint prediction becomes unstable. These are stress tests rather than additional main configurations. For example, the seed-1 mean ATE decreases from 0.092 m with joint predictions to 0.029 m with gating. The same pattern appears for CosPlace, BoQ, and DINOv2+SALAD. In the separate descriptor diagnostic, ordinary geometry gives online ATEs within approximately 0.048–0.053 m across the nine tested appearance cues, indicating substantially lower sensitivity to which historical frames were proposed.

sections.heading: M.6 What These Diagnostics Establish
sections.text: These experiments separate two decisions that are coupled in the default pipeline. The first is which local prediction to retain after the current and historical frames are processed together. The second is whether the verified historical measurement should revise the global trajectory . Revisit verification addresses the second decision but does not, by itself, protect the first. The joint policy used in the main experiments allows useful historical frames to improve the current prediction, as suggested by the CO3D comparison in Table S9 . However, the failure-case experiments show that an incorrect historical proposal can occasionally distort the local prediction before verification. Retaining the ordinary prediction removes this direct dependence, while gating provides an intermediate option that accepts only sufficiently small changes. The gate used here measures rotational disagreement only. It does not guarantee small translation, scale, or dense-point error. We adopt the gated policy with τ dist = 5 ∘ \tau_{\mathrm{dist}}=5^{\circ} as the default: on the default proposals it retains every joint prediction (Table S9 , where the largest measured distortion is 0.3 ∘ 0.3^{\circ} and the 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} gate matches the joint policy on both benchmarks), while the distortions in the failure cases of Table S10 are tens of degrees and are rejected. Finally, these results do not contradict the placement property in Appendix C . That property assumes that the local prediction has already been selected and then asks what happens when its global placement T k T_{k} changes. The present section instead studies the earlier question of whether joint processing changes the local prediction itself.

sections.heading: Appendix N Memory Growth and Pruning
sections.text: We additionally test retrieval as the memory bank grows using a separate retrieval-only diagnostic with up to 3,100 stored frames. A retrieved frame is considered a correct historical revisit when it comes from the same scene, lies within 10% of the scene’s spatial extent from the query camera, and differs in orientation by at most 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} . Recall@1 is the fraction of eligible queries for which such a revisit is ranked first, while Recall@5 measures whether one appears among the five highest-ranked retrievals. At 3,100 stored frames, scaffold retrieval achieves 0.36 Recall@1 compared with 0.25 for direct DINOv2 cosine retrieval, while Recall@5 is comparable at 0.42 versus 0.43. The stored bank also contains substantial redundancy. A simple pose-based insertion rule reduces the bank from 3,100 to 1,119 frames while preserving at least one valid historical revisit for 157 of the original 159 eligible queries. On these retained queries, scaffold Recall@5 increases from 0.42 to 0.54. This indicates that substantial redundancy can be removed without eliminating most useful historical observations, although we do not claim an optimal pruning strategy or unbounded memory capacity.

Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and subsequently align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from previous frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when subsequent observations reveal errors. To address these limitations, we introduce S caffold M em O ry for Re vision ( SMoRe ), a framework that equips existing geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMoRe associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. Crucially, SMoRe integrates with existing geometry foundation models while keeping them frozen, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. We evaluate SMoRe with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all the evaluated geometry models, SMoRe consistently improves long-sequence camera pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected camera poses and observations, SMoRe further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences. Code, data, and models will be publicly available upon publication. Figure 1: Limitations of existing 3D geometry models for long horizon and overview of our SMoRe . A Limitations. Feed-forward models process long sequences in separate windows and subsequently stitch their predictions, causing errors to accumulate at window boundaries and yielding inconsistent camera poses and 3D geometry. B Limitations. Video streaming models retain information across video frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when subsequent observations reveal errors, leading to persistent pose drift and distorted geometry over long sequences. C SMoRe Overview. SMoRe introduces four memory operations: Store retains frames, camera poses, and 3D point maps in the content bank, while the scaffold associates spatial and visual information. Retrieve uses the current frame’s visual descriptor to find candidate past frames. Verify jointly processes the current window and retrieved pairs to see whether their past poses support consistent window placement. Revise uses the accepted evidence to update the global placements of affected windows, moving their stored cameras and geometry together. 1 Introduction and Related Work Recovering camera motion and 3D scene structure from visual observations is fundamental to 3D computer vision, underpinning robotic navigation, autonomous systems, augmented reality, and embodied AI Shen et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026c) ; Piriyajitakonkij et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2018b) ; Zhang et al. (2018a) ; Khandelwal et al. (2023) . Recent geometry foundation models have made substantial progress toward this goal. DUSt3R ( Wang et al., 2024b ) introduced point-map regression for unified geometric inference without known camera calibration or poses, followed by MASt3R ( Leroy et al., 2024 ) , Fast3R ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , VGGT ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , VGGT- Ω \Omega ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , and π 3 \pi^{3} ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . These models estimate camera poses, depth, correspondences, and 3D scene structure directly from images. Yet, a fundamental challenge remains: how can they maintain accurate, spatially consistent reconstructions over long horizons? Existing geometry models largely approach long sequences in two ways, both with important limitations (Fig. 1 ). First, feed-forward models such as VGGT, VGGT- Ω \Omega , and π 3 \pi^{3} ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026b ) jointly infer geometry from groups of images. Long sequences are divided into fixed-length windows, reconstructed separately, and subsequently aligned into a common coordinate system. Small reconstruction or alignment errors can accumulate across windows, degrading camera poses and 3D geometry over long trajectories. TALO ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) and AMB3R ( Wang and Agapito, 2026 ) address this through submap alignment and compact volumetric representations, respectively, while VGGSfM ( Wang et al., 2024a ) and GlueMap ( Pan et al., 2026 ) combine learned geometry with structure-from-motion. Nevertheless, long-horizon reconstruction still requires maintaining geometric consistency across observations or submaps. Second, streaming geometry models such as CUT3R ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , StreamVGGT ( Zhuo et al., 2026 ) , and STream3R ( Lan et al., 2026 ) maintain information across successive observations through persistent states or causal caches. Such memory allows previous observations to inform future predictions, but retaining past context and explicitly revising previously estimated camera poses and scene geometry are different capabilities. Relatedly, EAGLE ( Cao et al., 2026 ) combines visual and geometric memory for visual-query localization in egocentric video, but does not target retrospective correction of long-horizon 3D reconstruction. Later observations may reveal that an earlier estimate was incorrect, yet existing streaming memory does not explicitly retrieve, verify, and revise that estimate. Thus, remembering the past is not equivalent to revising it. The need for retrospective correction is well established in simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), where errors are corrected through loop closure and global optimization, as in graph-based SLAM ( Grisetti et al., 2010 ; Strasdat et al., 2010 ) , ElasticFusion ( Whelan et al., 2015 ) , and ORB-SLAM3 ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Learned systems such as DROID-SLAM ( Teed and Deng, 2021 ) , NICER-SLAM ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) , and SLAMFormer ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) exploit geometric constraints across observations to correct accumulated errors. More recent works, including MASt3R-SLAM ( Murai et al., 2025 ) , VGGT-SLAM ( Maggio et al., 2025 ) , VGGT-SLAM++ ( Mandal et al., 2026 ) , and ViSTA-SLAM ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , combine learned geometry with loop closure, while VGGT-SLAM 2.0 ( Maggio and Carlone, 2026 ) uses model attention to verify retrieved images. However, these are dedicated SLAM systems built around specific representations and optimization pipelines. This motivates a general question: can existing geometry foundation models be equipped with a shared external memory to recall, verify, and revise past predictions while remaining frozen? Beyond computer vision, recurrent neural fields and continuous attractor networks (CANs) in neuroscience provide biologically inspired mechanisms for maintaining and representing continuous variables through persistent neural activity ( Amari, 1977 ; Burak and Fiete, 2009 ) . Vector-HaSH ( Chandra et al., 2025 ) further combines structured spatial representations with associative memory, linking spatial states with sensory observations. This principle suggests a natural way to organize long-horizon visual memory: associate where an observer is with what it observes, so that past observations can be retrieved when related spatial states are revisited. Building on this principle, we introduce S caffold M em O ry for Re vision ( SMoRe ), a revisable external memory for extending existing geometry foundation models to long-horizon inference. SMoRe goes beyond associative retrieval by supporting an explicit cycle of storage, retrieval, verification, and revision . As new observations arrive, SMoRe retrieves relevant past observations, compares them with current geometric evidence, verifies their consistency, and revises previously estimated poses and geometry when inconsistencies are detected. Corrected observations are retained in memory and can subsequently provide improved geometric context for later inference. Importantly, SMoRe is external to the geometry backbone. It therefore does not require a new geometry model to be trained for long-horizon processing. Instead, existing geometry foundation models can be integrated with SMoRe while their model weights remain frozen, requiring neither additional training nor fine-tuning. This design separates the problem of learning strong geometric priors from the problem of maintaining and correcting information over time: the foundation model provides geometric inference, while SMoRe provides persistent and revisable memory. Consequently, the same memory framework can be applied across different geometry backbones and tasks. We evaluate SMoRe with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across the evaluated geometry models, incorporating SMoRe consistently improves long-sequence camera pose estimation. It reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. The corrected poses and observations retained by SMoRe further improve the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. Our contributions are threefold: 1. Revisable external memory for long-horizon 3D geometry. We introduce SMoRe , an external memory that associates spatial context with visual observations and supports explicit storage, retrieval, geometric verification, and revision of previously estimated poses and scene structure. 2. Training-free integration with frozen geometry foundation models. SMoRe provides a model-agnostic interface for augmenting existing geometry foundation models while keeping their weights frozen, enabling long-horizon error correction without additional training or fine-tuning. 3. Comprehensive evaluation across models and 3D tasks. We evaluate SMoRe with eight geometry models on five datasets across camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, SLAM, and novel view synthesis, demonstrating consistent improvements in long-horizon geometric accuracy and spatial consistency. 2 Our Proposed S caffold M em O ry for Re vision ( SMoRe ) We introduce SMoRe , a revisable external memory for extending pretrained geometry foundation models to long-horizon inference (Fig. 1 ). SMoRe consists of a spatial scaffold and a content bank . The content bank stores past observations and their geometric predictions, while the scaffold associates where an observation was captured with what was observed through a shared memory representation. As new observations arrive, SMoRe stores their spatial and visual representations and uses visual content to retrieve candidate revisits. Because associative retrieval alone cannot determine whether a candidate is a genuine revisit, retrieved observations are verified against their historical poses before being used for correction. A verified revisit provides a global spatial anchor for revising accumulated placement errors. The geometry foundation model remains frozen throughout; only the external memory is updated online. Before describing these memory operations, we first define the overlapping frame windows used for local reconstruction and the local and global coordinate systems used to place and revise these reconstructions. Given RGB frames I 1 , … , I N I_{1},\ldots,I_{N} , we process them in overlapping windows 𝒲 k \mathcal{W}_{k} . By default, each window contains 32 frames, with 16 shared between consecutive windows. See Table S4 (Group G) for the effect of window size and overlap. Because a frame can appear in two overlapping windows, it is stored only once, using the first window in which it appears. We call this its source window , denoted src ⁡ ( i ) \operatorname{src}(i) for frame I i I_{i} . For each window, the geometry foundation model predicts camera poses and 3D point maps in a local coordinate system defined by the camera pose of the first frame in that window. We define the global coordinate system as that of the first window and let T k ∈ Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) T_{k}\in\mathrm{Sim}(3) denote the transformation that places 𝒲 k \mathcal{W}_{k} in this global coordinate system. Consecutive windows are initially placed by aligning the predicted camera poses of their overlapping frames. Camera poses and point maps remain stored in their source window’s local coordinate system, while T k T_{k} determines their global placement. The robust similarity alignment and the effect of changing T k T_{k} on stored geometry are detailed in Appendices B and C . 2.1 Associating Spatial and Visual Memory After processing each window, SMoRe stores its new frames in the content bank together with their predicted camera poses and point maps. Rather than storing global poses in a lookup table indexed by frame identity, SMoRe builds an associative memory : spatial states and visual observations are linked through a shared memory representation. This is important because, at retrieval time, the identity and location of a revisited frame are unknown. A new visual observation must therefore serve as a partial cue for recalling previously associated spatial information. Spatial scaffold. Following Vector-HaSH ( Chandra et al., 2025 ) , we represent each frame’s global camera pose using a structured spatial scaffold. Camera position is encoded by three periodic spatial modules operating at different spatial scales, while yaw, pitch, and roll are represented by three continuous attractor rings. The periodic representation preserves the continuous structure of position and orientation, while combining multiple spatial scales reduces the ambiguity introduced by any single periodic representation. Their concatenation forms the scaffold state 𝐠 i \mathbf{g}_{i} . We map 𝐠 i \mathbf{g}_{i} through a fixed random linear projection to a 1024-dimensional memory representation 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} , retaining only the 64 largest activations followed by normalization. This sparse intermediate representation is a deliberate design choice: activating only a small subset of memory units reduces interference among stored associations, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and making recall more robust to partial or noisy cues. We systematically vary the sparsity level and scaffold dimension and study their effects in Table S4 (Groups B and D). A reverse mapping, learned using ridge regression, reconstructs the spatial scaffold state from 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} . Thus, unlike a lookup table that can only return an entry given its explicit index, the scaffold supports associative reconstruction of spatial information from a shared memory state (see more analysis in Appendix J.1 and Table S4 (Group A)). See Appendix D for details of scaffold encoding and projection. Associating visual observations with the scaffold. To connect what is observed with where it was observed, we encode each frame I i I_{i} using a frozen DINOv2 ViT-S/14 encoder ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , yielding a normalized 384-dimensional visual descriptor 𝐬 i \mathbf{s}_{i} . We learn bidirectional associations between 𝐬 i \mathbf{s}_{i} and the shared memory representation 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} : visual content can cue its associated memory state, while the memory state can reconstruct its associated visual representation. Both mappings are updated incrementally using recursive least squares (RLS) whenever a new frame is stored. Together, these associations connect the spatial scaffold state 𝐠 i \mathbf{g}_{i} , shared memory representation 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} , and visual descriptor 𝐬 i \mathbf{s}_{i} . Consequently, a new visual observation can provide a partial cue for recalling memories associated with similar past observations, rather than requiring the identity or location of the corresponding frame to be known in advance. This associative recall is central to SMoRe : it enables what is currently observed to cue where related observations were previously encountered. Because such recall alone cannot establish that two observations correspond to the same physical location, we use it only to propose candidate revisits, which are subsequently verified geometrically (Sec. 2.2 ). All memory updates are external to the pretrained models; the geometry foundation model and DINOv2 encoder remain frozen. Instead of DINOv2, we evaluate alternative visual features in Appendix J.2 and Table S4 (Group C). 2.2 Retrieving and Verifying Revisits for Window Revision Retrieving candidate revisits based on visual feature similarity. Given a current frame I q I_{q} , we compute its visual descriptor 𝐬 q \mathbf{s}_{q} and use the learned visual association to obtain a query memory representation 𝐡 ~ q \widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{q} . Retrieval uses only visual information; the current camera pose and 3D geometry are not used. We do not directly trust the spatial state recalled from 𝐡 ~ q \widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{q} , because a novel observation may still activate an existing memory. Instead, we compare 𝐡 ~ q \widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{q} with all stored memory representations and select the five most similar frames. We then remove candidates that are within 64 frames of the current observation, originate from the immediately preceding window, or have DINOv2 cosine similarity below 0.5 0.5 . The remaining frames are treated as candidate revisits and are geometrically verified next. Full retrieval details are provided in Appendix D . Verifying revisits by historical pose consistency. For each retrieved candidate, we select a second nearby frame ( ± 3 \pm 3 frames) from the same source window to form a retrieved pair . We retain two pairs from different source windows, providing two independent historical references. If fewer than two valid pairs are available, no retrieval-based correction is applied. We use two pairs by default and study this choice in Table S4 (Group E). When two pairs are available, the geometry foundation model jointly processes the 32 current-window frames and four retrieved frames, placing all 36 frames in a common local coordinate system. The current window retains this joint prediction unless it rotates the current frames by more than 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} relative to the prediction from the current window alone, in which case the current-window prediction is kept and the joint pass serves only to measure the revisit (Appendix M ). Each retrieved pair connects this joint prediction to its previously placed source window and independently proposes a global placement for the current window, denoted T k ( a ) T_{k}^{(a)} and T k ( b ) T_{k}^{(b)} . We accept the revisit only if the two proposals are consistent in both rotation and translation: their rotational difference must be at most 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} , and their positional difference must be at most the spatial extent E k E_{k} of the current reconstruction (the median distance of its cameras from their centroid). Otherwise, the retrieval is rejected. Once verified, all four retrieved frames are jointly used to robustly estimate a single corrected global placement T k corr T_{k}^{\mathrm{corr}} . Importantly, T k corr T_{k}^{\mathrm{corr}} is fitted jointly from both historical references rather than obtained by averaging T k ( a ) T_{k}^{(a)} and T k ( b ) T_{k}^{(b)} . The alignment, verification, and corrected-placement formulations are provided in Appendix F . Progressive placement revision along the trajectory. The difference between the original placement T k T_{k} and corrected placement T k corr T_{k}^{\mathrm{corr}} represents the accumulated placement error revealed by the revisit. Rather than applying the correction abruptly to the current window, we progressively distribute it across the windows between the earlier historical reference and the current window. The historical reference remains fixed, intermediate windows receive increasingly larger corrections, and the current window receives the full correction. We interpolate these corrections in Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) ; the full formulation is provided in Appendix G . See Appendix J.3 and Table S4 (Group F) for an analysis of alternative placement revision strategies. Only the global placement of each affected window is revised. Its stored camera poses and point maps remain expressed in the local coordinate system of its source window and therefore move together under the updated global placement. 3 Experiments We evaluate all competitive baselines with and without SMoRe across five downstream tasks: camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. We perform three runs per experiment and aggregate results across runs. For each task, we describe the problem setting and datasets, followed by the compared methods, metrics, and results. Unless otherwise stated, all main-paper SMoRe results use only online retrieval, verification, and revision, without offline global optimization. We focus on this more challenging and practical setting, where corrections are made as observations arrive without access to the complete sequence. Results with offline pose-graph optimization are provided in Appendix J . 3.1 Camera Pose Estimation Problem setting and datasets. We evaluate long-horizon camera pose estimation on CO3Dv2 ( Reizenstein et al., 2021 ) and RealEstate10K (RE10K) ( Zhou et al., 2018 ) . CO3Dv2 contains object-centric videos spanning 8–68 s, with 200 annotated frames per sequence. RE10K contains predominantly forward-moving real-estate videos; we use 100 clips spanning 6.7–9.3 s. For both datasets, we uniformly sample N ∈ { 10 , 50 , 100 , 200 } N\in\{10,50,100,200\} frames from each trajectory. Baselines. We evaluate six feed-forward geometry foundation models: DUSt3R ( Wang et al., 2024b ) , Fast3R ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , MASt3R ( Leroy et al., 2024 ) , VGGT ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , VGGT- Ω \Omega ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , and π 3 \pi^{3} ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , together with two streaming models: StreamVGGT ( Zhuo et al., 2026 ) and STream3R ( Lan et al., 2026 ) . For each model, we compare its original camera predictions with those obtained using SMoRe on identical sampled frames. Feed-forward models use 32-frame windows with and without SMoRe . Streaming baselines use their native causal inference, while their SMoRe variants use the same 32-frame windowing policy. Metrics. We evaluate all pairs of sampled frames. For each pair, pose error is the larger of the rotation and translation-direction errors, so lower is better. AUC@30 instead measures the normalized area under the cumulative fraction of frame pairs whose pose error falls below thresholds up to 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} ; therefore, higher AUC@30 is better. Results. As shown in the right panel of Fig. 2 A, SMoRe consistently improves camera pose estimation on CO3Dv2, with nearly all points lying above the diagonal. The gains become more pronounced for longer sequences, with larger markers generally farther above the diagonal. At N = 200 N=200 , for example, VGGT improves from 90.0 to 93.9 AUC, VGGT- Ω \Omega from 91.6 to 94.7, and π 3 \pi^{3} from 89.9 to 93.3. On RE10K (left), the gains are smaller but remain evident across sequence lengths, including shorter trajectories. This is consistent with its predominantly forward camera motion providing fewer opportunities to revisit previously observed regions. Notably, some streaming baselines run out of memory (OOM) on longer sequences in both datasets, whereas the same models equipped with SMoRe successfully perform camera pose estimation through memory-efficient windowed processing (crosses in Fig. 2 A). We evaluate multi-view depth estimation on Replica ( Straub et al., 2019 ) and 3D point-cloud reconstruction on ScanNet++ ( Yeshwanth et al., 2023 ) . Replica contains 18 photorealistic synthetic indoor environments with approximately 2,000 frames per scene, providing long camera trajectories and dense reference geometry for multi-view depth evaluation. ScanNet++ contains 1,006 high-fidelity real-world indoor scenes with high-resolution RGB observations and laser-scanned reference geometry, with long sequences spanning each indoor environment. For both datasets, we process the sequences using the 32-frame windowing strategy in Sec. 2 . These long sequences require reconstruction across many successive windows, providing a challenging setting for evaluating whether SMoRe can reduce accumulated geometric inconsistencies through revisited observations. Baselines. We use the same eight geometry models (Sec. 3.1 ), comparing each baseline with its SMoRe counterpart. Metrics. We report reconstruction accuracy, completeness, and overall error in centimetres. Accuracy measures the distance from reconstructed to reference geometry, while completeness measures the reverse direction. Overall error is their mean; lower is better. Results. Table 1 shows consistent improvements with SMoRe across all eight geometry models on both datasets when evaluated over full trajectories. On Replica, SMoRe reduces overall Chamfer error by approximately 58% across the evaluated models. For example, VGGT improves from 9.15 to 2.49 cm and VGGT- Ω \Omega from 7.50 to 2.00 cm. Streaming models also exhibit marked gains (e.g., StreamVGGT overall error drops from 6.65 to 1.84 cm on Replica and from 17.80 to 4.50 cm on ScanNet++). These results confirm that revising previously placed window reconstructions with SMoRe successfully resolves accumulated drift over long sequences. We evaluate SLAM on all seven indoor scenes of 7-Scenes ( Shotton et al., 2013 ) , where the objective is to estimate the camera trajectory while reconstructing the environment from an incoming video stream. Each sequence contains 17–33 s of continuous video, providing long trajectories for evaluating accumulated drift and revisit-driven correction. Baselines. We report absolute trajectory error (ATE) RMSE in metres after similarity alignment between the estimated and ground-truth camera trajectories. We evaluate novel view synthesis on 7-Scenes ( Shotton et al., 2013 ) and CO3Dv2 ( Reizenstein et al., 2021 ) , where input views from long sequences are used to render scenes from unseen viewpoints. Every eighth keyframe is held out for evaluation and excluded from geometry prediction. We evaluate 156 held-out views on 7-Scenes and 888 on CO3Dv2 (Appendix H.5 ). Baselines. We compare VGGT- Ω \Omega , VGGT, π 3 \pi^{3} , STream3R, Fast3R, and StreamVGGT ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Lan et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Zhuo et al., 2026 ) . For each geometry model, we train separate 3D Gaussian decoders using geometry from chained consecutive windows (Baseline) and SMoRe , respectively. For fair comparison, both decoders share the same architecture, training data, schedule, and random seed. Each decoder renders target views from eight nearby input keyframes, while the geometry models remain frozen. Decoders are trained on 7-Scenes sequences disjoint from test trajectories and transferred to CO3Dv2 without further fine-tuning (Appendix I ). Metrics. We report PSNR ( ↑ \uparrow ), SSIM ( ↑ \uparrow ), and LPIPS ( ↓ \downarrow ). To assess long-horizon consistency, we additionally analyze target views whose source keyframes span multiple visits to the same region (Appendix H.5 ). Results. As shown in Table 2 , SMoRe improves all three metrics across all six geometry models on 7-Scenes, with larger gains for revisited targets (Appendix I ). On CO3Dv2, VGGT- Ω \Omega , VGGT, π 3 \pi^{3} , and StreamVGGT achieve PSNR gains of 0.34–0.64 dB with SMoRe , alongside improvements in SSIM and LPIPS. STream3R and Fast3R achieve comparable PSNR with and without SMoRe , while improving SSIM and LPIPS with SMoRe . These smaller gains may reflect residual errors in local geometric predictions that cannot be corrected through window placement revision alone. Qualitative examples are shown in Fig. 2 B and Fig. S2 . In Fig. 2 B, for example, VGGT- Ω \Omega + SMoRe better preserves the geometry and appearance of the headphone than VGGT- Ω \Omega alone. More generally, the improved geometry yields sharper object boundaries and better-preserved object structure in the synthesized views.
